p.seg: Thus I have heard.
At one time the Buddha was in the Amrapali Grove in the city of Vaishālī.
He was accompanied by eight thousand great bhikshus.
There were thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas
who were well known to the assembly,
all accomplished in great wisdom and fundamental practices,
established by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas.
They guarded the citadel of the Dharma and upheld the true teaching,
able to roar like lions, their fame spreading throughout the ten directions.
They befriended sentient beings without being asked and brought them peace.
They continued and glorified the Three Jewels, ensuring their unbroken lineage.
They subdued demonic adversaries and restrained all non-Buddhist paths.
All were purified, forever free from afflictions and hindrances.
Their minds constantly abided in unobstructed liberation.
Their mindfulness, concentration, spiritual powers, and eloquence were unceasing.
Generosity, moral discipline, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom,
along with skillful means, were all fully perfected.
They attained the patient acceptance of non-arising dharmas, realizing nothing is attained.
They skillfully followed and turned the irreversible wheel.
They well understood the characteristics of dharmas and knew the faculties of sentient beings.
They overshadowed the great assembly with fearlessness.
They cultivated their minds with merits and wisdom.
Adorned with magnificent marks, their forms and appearances were supreme.
They renounced all worldly adornments and attachments.
Their renown soared high, surpassing Mount Sumeru.
Their profound faith was firm and unyielding like a vajra.
The Dharma treasure shone universally, raining sweet dew.
Among all voices, theirs were supremely subtle and excellent.
They penetrated deeply into dependent origination, cutting off all wrong views.
They transcended the two extremes of existence and non-existence, with no residual habits.
Expounding the Dharma fearlessly, like a lion's roar,
their teachings resounded like thunder.
Immeasurable, they surpassed all measures.
They gathered all Dharma treasures like an ocean-guiding teacher.
They thoroughly comprehended the profound and subtle meanings of all dharmas.
They skillfully knew the destinations of sentient beings' rebirths and the activities of their minds.
They approached the peerless wisdom, sovereign powers, ten strengths, and eighteen unique qualities of the Buddha.
They closed all gates to the evil destinies,
yet manifested in the five paths to show their forms.
As great healing kings, they skillfully cured all afflictions,
prescribing medicines according to the illness, enabling beings to practice.
Innumerable merits were all accomplished.
Innumerable Buddha lands were all purified and adorned.
Those who saw or heard them all received benefits.
All their actions were never in vain.
Thus, all such merits were fully perfected.
Their names were: Bodhisattva Equal Contemplation,
Bodhisattva Unequal Contemplation,
Bodhisattva Equal and Unequal Contemplation,
Bodhisattva King of Samādhi Mastery,
Bodhisattva King of Dharma Mastery,
Bodhisattva Dharma Mark,
Bodhisattva Light Mark,
Bodhisattva Light Adornment,
Bodhisattva Great Adornment,
Bodhisattva Jewel Accumulation,
Bodhisattva Eloquence Accumulation,
Bodhisattva Jewel Hand,
Bodhisattva Jewel Seal Hand,
Bodhisattva Constantly Raised Hand,
Bodhisattva Constantly Lowered Hand,
Bodhisattva Constant Compassion,
Bodhisattva Joyful Root,
Bodhisattva Joyful King,
Bodhisattva Eloquent Sound,
Bodhisattva Space Treasury,
Bodhisattva Holder of the Jewel Torch,
Bodhisattva Jewel Courage,
Bodhisattva Jewel Sight,
Bodhisattva Indra's Net,
Bodhisattva Bright Net,
Bodhisattva Non-conditioned Contemplation,
Bodhisattva Wisdom Accumulation,
Bodhisattva Jewel Victory,
Bodhisattva Heavenly King,
Bodhisattva Destroyer of Demons,
Bodhisattva Lightning Virtue,
Bodhisattva Sovereign King,
Bodhisattva Merit Mark Adornment,
Bodhisattva Lion's Roar,
Bodhisattva Thunder Sound,
Bodhisattva Sound of Clashing Mountains,
Bodhisattva Fragrant Elephant,
Bodhisattva White Fragrant Elephant,
Bodhisattva Constant Vigor,
Bodhisattva Unceasing,
Bodhisattva Wondrous Birth,
Bodhisattva Flower Adornment,
Bodhisattva Guānshìyīn,
Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
Bodhisattva Brahma's Net,
Bodhisattva Jewel Staff,
Bodhisattva Unsurpassed,
Bodhisattva Land Adornment,
Bodhisattva Golden Topknot,
Bodhisattva Pearl Topknot,
Bodhisattva Maitreya,
Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Dharma Prince,
and so on, thirty-two thousand in all.
Furthermore, there were ten thousand Brahma kings such as Śikhin,
who came from the other four continents to the Buddha's place to hear the Dharma.
There were also twelve thousand heavenly emperors,
also from the other four continents, seated in the assembly.
Along with other powerfully majestic devas,
dragons,
yakkhas,
gandharvas,
asuras,
garuḍas,
kiṃnaras,
mahoragas,
and others all came to the assembly.
Bhikshus, bhikshuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās all came to the assembly.
At that time, the Buddha, surrounded reverently by immeasurable hundreds of thousands, was expounding the Dharma.
Like Mount Sumeru king manifesting in the great ocean,
he was seated securely on a lion throne of various jewels,
overshadowing all the assembled multitude.
At that time, in the city of Vaishālī, there was a elder's son
named Jewel Accumulation,
accompanied by five hundred elders' sons,
holding seven-jeweled canopies, came to the Buddha's place.
They bowed their heads at his feet,
and each offered their canopies to the Buddha.
Through the Buddha's majestic power, all the jeweled canopies merged into one canopy,
covering the entire three-thousandfold great thousand world system.
The vast and extensive features of this world all appeared within it.
Moreover, in this three-thousandfold great thousand world system,
all the Mount Sumerus, Snow Mountains,
Mount Mucilinda, Great Mount Mucilinda,
Fragrant Mountains, Jewel Mountains, Golden Mountains, Black Mountains,
Iron Encircling Mountains, Great Iron Encircling Mountains,
great seas, rivers, streams, and springs,
as well as the sun, moon, and stars,
heavenly palaces, dragon palaces,
and palaces of various revered spirits,
all appeared within the jeweled canopy.
Also, the Buddhas of the ten directions and their Dharma expounding appeared within the jeweled canopy.
Then the entire assembly,
witnessing the Buddha's spiritual power, exclaimed at this unprecedented sight.
They joined their palms, bowed to the Buddha, gazing at his honorable countenance without blinking.
Thereupon, the elder's son Jewel Accumulation,
right before the Buddha, expressed his praise in verse:
Your eyes pure, long, and broad like blue lotuses,
Your mind purified, having transcended all meditative states,
Long accumulated pure karma, praised as immeasurable,
Guiding beings to tranquility, I bow to you.
Having seen the great sage's spiritual transformations,
Universally revealing immeasurable lands in the ten directions,
Wherein all Buddhas expound the Dharma,
All this is seen and heard by everyone.
The Dharma King's power surpasses all beings,
Constantly bestowing the wealth of Dharma upon all,
Skillfully discerning the characteristics of dharmas,
Yet unmoving in the supreme meaning.
Having mastered all dharmas with sovereignty,
Therefore I bow to this Dharma King.
Expounding Dharma not as existent nor non-existent,
All dharmas arise due to causes and conditions,
No self, no doer, no experiencer,
Yet the karma of good and evil does not perish.
Initially, at the bodhi tree, with power subduing demons,
Attaining nectar-like cessation, awakening accomplished,
Devoid of mind, consciousness, and sensations,
Yet completely crushing all non-Buddhist paths.
Turning the Dharma wheel three times in the great thousand,
The wheel originally ever pure,
Devas and humans attaining the Path bear witness,
Thus the Three Jewels appear in the world.
With this wondrous Dharma aiding sentient beings,
Once receiving it,不退转, ever tranquil,
Healing aging, sickness, and death, the great healing king,
Should be revered, his Dharma ocean's virtues boundless.
Unmoved by slander or praise like Mount Sumeru,
With equal compassion toward good and evil,
Mind acting impartially like space itself,
Who hearing of this human jewel would not revere?
Now I offer this humble canopy to the World-Honored One,
Within it appears my three-thousandfold world,
Palaces where devas, dragons, and spirits dwell,
Gandharvas, yakkhas, and others,
All see everything in the world,
The Tathāgata's compassionate display of these transformations,
The assembly beholds this rarity and praises the Buddha.
Now I bow to the Honored One of the three realms,
The great sage Dharma King, refuge of all,
With purified minds contemplating the Buddha, all rejoice,
Each sees the World-Honored One before them,
This is the unique power of spiritual mastery.
The Buddha expounds the Dharma with one voice,
Beings understand according to their kind,
Each thinks the World-Honored One speaks their language,
This is the unique power of spiritual mastery.
The Buddha expounds the Dharma with one voice,
Beings each comprehend according to their understanding,
All receive and practice, gaining benefits,
This is the unique power of spiritual mastery.
The Buddha expounds the Dharma with one voice,
Some feel fear, some joy,
Some generate renunciation, some resolve doubts,
This is the unique power of spiritual mastery.
I bow to the Great Vigorous One of the Ten Powers.
I bow to the One who has attained Fearlessness.
I bow to the One abiding in Incomparable Dharma.
I bow to the Great Guide of all.
I bow to the One who severs all bonds and fetters.
I bow to the One who has reached the Other Shore.
I bow to the One who ferries across all worlds.
I bow to the One forever freed from the path of birth and death.
Fully knowing the comings and goings of all beings,
Skillfully attaining liberation in all dharmas,
Unattached to the world like a lotus flower,
Constantly well-entered into the practice of emptiness and tranquility,
Penetrating the marks of all dharmas without obstruction,
I bow to the One like space, with nothing to rely upon.
At that time, the elder's son Bǎojī,
having spoken this verse, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
these five hundred elders' sons
have all aroused the mind of Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi.
We wish to hear about attaining the purity of the Buddha-land.
We beseech the World-Honored One
to explain the practices of Bodhisattvas for purifying the land."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, Bǎojī,
that you can ask the Tathāgata about the practices for purifying the land for the sake of Bodhisattvas.
Listen carefully, ponder well,
and I shall explain it to you."
Thereupon Bǎojī and the five hundred elders' sons
received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"Bǎojī,
the various classes of beings are the Buddha-land of the Bodhisattva.
Why is this?
The Bodhisattva acquires a Buddha-land according to the beings he transforms.
He acquires a Buddha-land according to the beings he tames.
He acquires a Buddha-land according to the country through which beings enter the Buddha's wisdom.
He acquires a Buddha-land according to the country through which beings develop Bodhisattva roots.
Why is this?
The Bodhisattva's acquisition of a pure land
is entirely for the benefit of all beings.
It is like someone wishing to build a palace on open ground, accomplishing it without hindrance.
But if attempted in empty space, it ultimately cannot be achieved.
So it is with the Bodhisattva:
for the sake of accomplishing beings, he vows to acquire a Buddha-land.
Vowing to acquire a Buddha-land is not done in emptiness.
Bǎojī,
you should know that a straightforward mind is the pure land of the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, beings free from flattery will be born in his land.
A profound mind is the pure land of the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, beings complete with merits will be born in his land.
The mind of Bodhi is the pure land of the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, Mahayana beings will be born in his land.
Giving is the pure land of the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, beings capable of relinquishing all will be born in his land.
Moral discipline is the pure land of the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, beings who practice the ten good paths and fulfill their vows will be born in his land.
Forbearance is the pure land of the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, beings adorned with the thirty-two marks will be born in his land.
Vigor is the pure land of the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, beings diligent in cultivating all merits will be born in his land.
Meditation is the pure land of the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, beings with collected and unconfused minds will be born in his land.
Wisdom is the pure land of the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, beings in correct concentration will be born in his land.
The four immeasurable minds are the pure land of the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, beings accomplished in kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity will be born in his land.
The four means of attraction are the pure land of the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, beings guided by liberation will be born in his land.
Skillful means is the pure land of the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, beings with unobstructed skillful means in all dharmas will be born in his land.
The thirty-seven aids to enlightenment are the pure land of the Bodhisattva.

When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, beings of the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of psychic power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the noble path will be born in his land.
The mind of dedication is the pure land of the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, he will attain a land complete with all merits.
Explaining the removal of the eight difficulties is the pure land of the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, his land will be free from the three evil paths and the eight difficulties.
Guarding one's own precepts and not criticizing others' faults is the pure land of the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, his land will have no name for transgressing prohibitions.
The ten good deeds are the pure land of the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, his life will not be cut short,
he will be greatly wealthy, practice purity, speak truthfully,
always use gentle words, and his retinue will not leave him.
He will skillfully reconcile disputes and his words will be beneficial.
Beings free from jealousy and anger, with right view, will be born in his land.
Thus, Bǎojī,
according to the Bodhisattva's straightforward mind, he can initiate practice.
According to his practice, he attains a profound mind.
According to his profound mind,
his mind becomes tamed.
According to his tamed mind, he practices as taught.
According to practicing as taught, he can dedicate.
According to his dedication, he possesses skillful means.
According to his skillful means, he accomplishes beings.
According to accomplishing beings, the Buddha-land becomes pure.
According to the purity of the Buddha-land, the teaching becomes pure.
According to the purity of the teaching, wisdom becomes pure.
According to the purity of wisdom, his mind becomes pure.
According to the purity of his mind, all merits become pure.
Therefore, Bǎojī,
if a Bodhisattva wishes to attain a pure land, he should purify his mind.
As his mind is purified, the Buddha-land becomes purified."
At that time, Śāriputra,
empowered by the Buddha's might, thought thus:
"If the Bodhisattva's mind is pure then the Buddha-land is pure,
then when our World-Honored One was a Bodhisattva, was his mind not pure,
that this Buddha-land is so impure?"
The Buddha, knowing his thought, immediately said to him:
"What do you think?
Are the sun and moon not pure?
Yet the blind do not see them."
He replied, "No,
World-Honored One.
It is the fault of the blind, not the fault of the sun and moon."
"Śāriputra,
due to the offenses of beings, they do not see the majestic purity of the Tathāgata's Buddha-land.
It is not the Tathāgata's fault.
Śāriputra,
my land is pure, but you do not see it."
Then the Brahmā king with spiral topknot said to Śāriputra:
"Do not think thus,
considering this Buddha-land to be impure.
Why?
I see the land of Śākyamuni Buddha as pure,
like the palace of the Maheśvara heaven."
Śāriputra said:
"I see this land
with hills, hollows, thorns, gravel,
stones, mountains, and filth everywhere."
The Brahmā king with spiral topknot said:
"Sir, your mind has highs and lows,
not relying on the Buddha's wisdom.
Therefore you see this land as impure.
Śāriputra,
the Bodhisattva regards all beings
entirely as equal,
with a profoundly pure mind.
Relying on the Buddha's wisdom, he can see this Buddha-land as pure."
Thereupon the Buddha pressed the ground with his toe,
and immediately the three-thousand great thousand worlds were adorned with hundreds of thousands of precious jewels,
like the land of Jewel Adornment Buddha, adorned with immeasurable merits and jewels.
The entire assembly exclaimed at this unprecedented sight,
and each saw himself seated on a jeweled lotus.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"You now behold the majestic purity of this Buddha-land."
Śāriputra said:
"So it is, World-Honored One.
What I never saw before,
what I never heard before,
now the majestic purity of the Buddha-land is fully revealed."
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"My Buddha-land is always pure like this.
But to save those inferior people,
I display this land of various evils and impurities.
It is like gods eating from the same jeweled vessel, yet the color of their food differs according to their merits.
So it is, Śāriputra.
If a person's mind is pure, he will see the merits and adornments of this land."
When the Buddha manifested the majestic purity of this land,
the five hundred elders' sons led by Bǎojī all attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas.
Eighty-four thousand people all aroused the mind of Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi.
The Buddha withdrew his supernatural power,
and then the world returned to its former state.
Thirty-two thousand gods and humans seeking the Śrāvaka vehicle
understood that all conditioned dharmas are impermanent,
became free from dust and defilement, and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Eight thousand bhikṣus, not accepting any dharmas, were freed from outflows and their minds liberated.
At that time, in the great city of Vaiśālī, there was an elder named Vimalakīrti,
who had already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, deeply planting roots of goodness.
He had attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas.
His eloquence was unobstructed.
He sported with spiritual powers and mastered all dhāraṇīs.
He attained fearlessness, subdued the toils of Māra.
He entered the profound Dharma-gate and was skilled in the perfection of wisdom.
He was accomplished in skillful means and great vows.
He clearly understood the inclinations of beings' minds.
He could also distinguish the sharpness or dullness of their faculties.
Long devoted to the Buddha-way, his mind was pure and resolved on the Mahayana.
In all his actions, he could skillfully contemplate.
He dwelt in the Buddha's dignity, his mind vast as the ocean.
He was praised by the Buddhas,
respected by Śakra, Brahmā, and world-protectors.
To save people, he dwelled in Vaiśālī with skillful means.
His wealth was immeasurable, gathering the poor.
His observance of precepts was pure, gathering those who broke precepts.
With forbearance regulating his conduct, he gathered the angry.
With great vigor, he gathered the lazy.
With single-minded meditative tranquility, he gathered the distracted.
With resolute wisdom, he gathered the ignorant.
Though a layman, he upheld the pure precepts of the śramaṇa.
Though dwelling at home, he was unattached to the three realms.
He showed he had wife and children, yet constantly practiced purity.
He appeared to have retinue, yet always delighted in solitude.
Though wearing jewels, he adorned his body with marks and features.
Though eating and drinking, he took meditation joy as flavor.
If he went to gambling or entertainment places, it was to save people.
He associated with various heterodox paths without harming his right faith.
Though versed in worldly texts, he always delighted in the Buddha-Dharma.
He was revered by all and received the highest offerings.
Upholding the true Dharma, he guided both young and old.
In all his dealings and interactions, though he gained worldly profits, he did not rejoice in them.
He traveled through the city's thoroughfares, benefiting all beings.
Entering the halls of governance, he protected and aided everyone.
In places of discourse, he guided with the Great Vehicle.
In schools, he instructed and enlightened the young.
Entering brothels, he revealed the faults of desire.
In taverns, he helped others establish their resolve.
Among elders, he was honored and taught them the supreme Dharma.
Among householders, he was honored and severed their attachments and greed.
Among kṣatriyas, he was honored and taught them patience and forbearance.
Among brāhmaṇas, he was honored and removed their arrogance.
Among ministers, he was honored and instructed them in the true Dharma.
Among princes, he was honored and showed them loyalty and filial piety.
Among palace officials, he was honored and transformed the palace women.
Among commoners, he was honored and encouraged them to cultivate blessings.
Among Brahmā gods, he was honored and taught them superior wisdom.
Among Śakra devas, he was honored and revealed impermanence to them.
Among world-protectors, he was honored and protected all beings.
The elder Vimalakīrti,
through such immeasurable skillful means, benefited countless beings.
Through his expedient means, he manifested an illness.
Because of his illness,
kings, ministers, elders, householders, brāhmaṇas,
and various princes along with other officials,
countless thousands, all came to inquire about his health.
Those who came,
Vimalakīrti used his own illness to extensively expound the Dharma.
O virtuous ones,
this body is impermanent, without strength, without power, and without solidity.
It is a quickly decaying thing that cannot be trusted.
It is suffering and affliction, a gathering place for all illnesses.
O virtuous ones,
a wise person does not rely on such a body.
This body is like a mass of foam that cannot be grasped.
This body is like a bubble that cannot endure long.
This body is like a flame, born from craving.
This body is like a plantain tree, hollow within and without firmness.
This body is like an illusion, arising from inverted views.
This body is like a dream, a false perception.
This body is like a shadow, appearing due to karmic conditions.
This body is like an echo, dependent on causes and conditions.
This body is like a floating cloud, instantly changing and vanishing.
This body is like lightning, thought after thought without abiding.
This body has no master, like the earth.
This body has no self, like fire.
This body has no life, like the wind.
This body has no person, like water.
This body is unreal, with the four elements as its home.
This body is empty, devoid of self and what belongs to self.
This body is without consciousness, like grass, trees, tiles, or stones.
This body does not act, moved by the force of wind.
This body is impure, filled with filth and defilement.
This body is false and deceptive.
Though bathed, clothed, and fed, it is destined for destruction.
This body is a calamity, afflicted with a hundred and one illnesses.
This body is like a crumbling well, oppressed by old age.
This body is uncertain and bound for death.
This body is like a poisonous snake, a vengeful enemy, an empty village.
Composed of the aggregates, sense realms, and entrances.
O virtuous ones,
This body should be regarded with disgust; one should take delight in the Buddha's body.
Why is that?
The Buddha's body is the Dharma body.
It arises from immeasurable merit and wisdom.
It arises from precepts, meditation, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge of liberation.
It arises from compassion, loving-kindness, joy, and equanimity.
It arises from giving, moral discipline, patience, gentleness, diligent practice, meditation, liberation, samādhi, learning, wisdom, and the pāramitās.
It arises from skillful means.
It arises from the six supernatural powers.
It arises from the three clear knowledges.
It arises from the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment.
It arises from calm and insight.
It arises from the ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and eighteen unique qualities.
It arises from the cessation of all unwholesome dharmas and the accumulation of all wholesome dharmas.
It arises from truth.
It arises from diligence.
From such immeasurable pure dharmas arises the Tathāgata's body.
O virtuous ones,
If you wish to attain the Buddha's body and eradicate the illnesses of all beings,
you should generate the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Thus, the elder Vimalakīrti,
for those inquiring about his illness, taught the Dharma accordingly.
Causing countless thousands to generate the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti thought to himself,
"Lying ill in bed,
will the World-Honored One, out of great compassion, not take pity on me?"
The Buddha knew his thought,
and said to Śāriputra,
"You go to Vimalakīrti to inquire about his illness."
Śāriputra said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One,
I am not fit to go and inquire about his illness.
Why is that?
I recall once sitting in meditation under a tree in a forest.
Then Vimalakīrti came and said to me,
'O Śāriputra,
sitting in this way is not necessarily true meditation.
For true meditation
does not manifest body or mind within the three realms—
that is true meditation.
Not arising from the cessation concentration yet displaying all dignified manners—
that is true meditation.
Not abandoning the Dharma of the path yet engaging in ordinary affairs—
that is true meditation.
The mind neither abiding within nor without—
that is true meditation.
Unmoved by all views yet practicing the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment—
that is true meditation.
Not cutting off afflictions yet entering nirvāṇa—
that is true meditation.
If one can sit in this way,
the Buddha will seal it with approval.'
At that time, World-Honored One,
hearing these words, I fell silent and could not respond.
Therefore, I am not fit to go and inquire about his illness."
The Buddha said to Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
"You go to Vimalakīrti to inquire about his illness."
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One,
I am not fit to go and inquire about his illness.
Why is that?
I recall once entering the great city of Vaiśālī
and teaching the Dharma to householders in the streets.
Then Vimalakīrti came and said to me,
'O Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
when teaching the Dharma to white-robed householders,
you should not do so as you are now.
One who teaches the Dharma should teach in accordance with the Dharma.
The Dharma has no beings, for it is free from the defilement of beings.
The Dharma has no self, for it is free from the defilement of self.
The Dharma has no life, for it is free from birth and death.
The Dharma has no person, for the past and future are cut off.
The Dharma is always tranquil, for it extinguishes all characteristics.
The Dharma is beyond characteristics, for it has no object of reliance.
The Dharma has no name, for words and speech are cut off.
The Dharma has no explanation, for it is beyond conceptual thinking.
The Dharma has no form, like empty space.
The Dharma is beyond debate, for it is ultimately empty.
The Dharma has no 'mine,' for it is free from what is mine.
The Dharma has no discrimination, for it is free from all consciousness.
The Dharma has no comparison, for it is without relative existence.
The Dharma is not dependent on causes, nor does it abide in conditions.
The Dharma is identical with the nature of dharmas, entering all dharmas.
The Dharma follows thusness, yet there is nothing to follow.
The Dharma abides in reality, unmoved by extremes.
The Dharma is unshakable, not relying on the six sense objects.
The Dharma neither comes nor goes, always non-abiding.
The Dharma accords with emptiness, follows signlessness, and corresponds to wishlessness.
The Dharma is beyond beauty and ugliness.
The Dharma neither increases nor decreases.
The Dharma has no birth or death.
The Dharma has no abode.
The Dharma is beyond the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The Dharma has no high or low.
The Dharma eternally abides unmoved.
The Dharma is beyond all contemplation and practice.
O Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
such being the nature of the Dharma, how can it be spoken of?
One who teaches the Dharma has nothing to say or show.
One who listens to the Dharma hears nothing and gains nothing.
It is like an illusory person teaching the Dharma to illusory beings.
With this understanding, one should teach the Dharma.
One should discern whether beings' faculties are sharp or dull,
be skilled in knowledge and free from obstructions,
praise the Great Vehicle with a mind of great compassion,
remember to repay the Buddha's kindness and preserve the Three Jewels,
and then teach the Dharma.'
When Vimalakīrti spoke this Dharma,
eight hundred householders generated the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
I lack such eloquence,
therefore I am not fit to go and inquire about his illness."
The Buddha said to Mahākāśyapa,
"You go to Vimalakīrti to inquire about his illness."
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One,
I am not fit to go and inquire about his illness.
Why is that?
I recall once begging for alms in a poor district.
Then Vimalakīrti came and said to me,
'O Mahākāśyapa,
you have a compassionate heart, but it is not universal.
You abandon the wealthy and beg only from the poor.
Kāśyapa,
abide in the Dharma of equality and beg for food in sequence.
For the sake of not eating, you should beg for food.
To break the notion of composite things, you should receive material food.
Without accepting, you should accept that food.
Enter the village with the thought of an empty gathering.
See forms as equal to a blind person.
Hear sounds as equal to an echo.
Smell odors as equal to the wind.
Taste flavors without discrimination.
Experience touches as in wisdom realization.
Know all dharmas as illusory, without self-nature or other-nature.
Originally unarisen, now unceasing.'
Jiāyè.
If one can refrain from abandoning the eight wrong paths yet enter the eight liberations,
using erroneous appearances to enter the true Dharma,
offering one meal to all beings,
making offerings to all Buddhas, sages, and worthies,
only then may one partake of food.
Eating in this way is neither with afflictions nor separate from afflictions.
Neither entering meditative concentration nor arising from it,
neither abiding in the world nor abiding in nirvana.
For the giver, there is neither great merit nor small merit,
neither benefit nor harm.
This is the true entry into the Buddha Way, not relying on the Śrāvaka path.
Jiāyè,
if one eats in this manner, they do not consume others' offerings in vain.
At that time, O World-Honored One,
hearing these words, I attained what I had never had before,
and immediately felt deep reverence for all Bodhisattvas.
I further thought to myself:
"This householder possesses such eloquence and wisdom that he can speak thus.
Who, upon hearing this, would not aspire to attain Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi?"
From then on, I ceased urging others to follow the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha paths.
Therefore, I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
The Buddha said to Xūpútí,
"You go visit Wéimójié and inquire about his illness."
Xūpútí said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One,
I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
Why is this?
I recall once entering his house to beg for food.
At that time, Wéimójié took my bowl and filled it with rice,
then said to me,
'O Xūpútí,
if you can regard food as equal, then all dharmas are also equal;
if all dharmas are equal, then food is also equal.
Only by begging in this manner may you accept food.
Xūpútí,
without severing lust, anger, and ignorance, yet not abiding with them either;
without destroying the body, yet following the one mark;
without extinguishing ignorance and craving, yet giving rise to clarity and liberation;
attaining liberation through the marks of the five heinous crimes;
neither bound nor liberated;
not seeing the Four Truths, yet not failing to see the Truths;
neither attaining the fruit nor failing to attain it;
neither an ordinary person nor apart from ordinary ways;
neither a sage nor not a sage;
though accomplishing all dharmas, yet detached from the marks of all dharmas—
only then may you accept food.
Xūpútí,
if you do not see the Buddha nor hear the Dharma,
and those six teachers of heterodox paths—
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa,
Maskarī Gośālīputra,
Sañjaya Vairaṭīputra,
Ajita Keśakambala,
Kakuda Kātyāyana,
Nirgrantha Jñātiputra, and others—
are your teachers, under whom you have left home,
and you follow them in their falls,
only then may you accept food.
Xūpútí,
if you enter all wrong views without reaching the other shore,
dwell in the eight difficulties without attaining the state of no difficulty,
identify with afflictions yet separate from pure dharmas;
if you have attained the samādhi of non-contention,
yet all beings have also attained this samādhi;
those who give to you are not fields of merit;
those who make offerings to you fall into the three evil realms;
if you join hands with Māras as their companions in toil,
and you are no different from the Māras and all defilements;
if you harbor enmity toward all beings,
slander the Buddhas, destroy the Dharma, and are excluded from the assembly—
never attaining final nirvana—
only if you are thus may you accept food.'
At that time, O World-Honored One,
hearing these words, I was bewildered and did not understand what he was saying,
nor did I know how to respond.
I set down the bowl and was about to leave his house,
when Wéimójié said,
'O Xūpútí, take your bowl and do not fear.
What do you think?
If a transformation created by the Tathāgata
were questioned about such matters,
would it fear?'
I said,
'No.'
Wéimójié said,
'All dharmas are like illusory transformations.
You should not fear now.
Why?
All speech does not depart from this characteristic.
As for the wise, they do not cling to words and thus have no fear.
Why?
The nature of words is detached; there are no words.
This is liberation.
The mark of liberation is all dharmas.'
When Wéimójié spoke this Dharma,
two hundred devas attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Therefore, I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
The Buddha said to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra,
"You go visit Wéimójié and inquire about his illness."
Pūrṇa said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One,
I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
Why is this?
I recall once being in a great forest, under a tree,
expounding the Dharma to some newly ordained bhikṣus.
At that time, Wéimójié came and said to me,
'O Pūrṇa,
you should first enter samādhi to observe the minds of these people before expounding the Dharma.
Do not place impure food in a precious vessel.
You should know what these bhikṣus are contemplating.
Do not equate lapis lazuli with crystal.
You cannot discern the roots of beings,
so do not expound the Śrāvaka vehicle.
They have no wounds; do not injure them.
If you wish to tread the great path, do not show them bypaths.
Do not pour the great ocean into a cow's hoof-print.
Do not equate the sun's light with that of a firefly.
Pūrṇa,
these bhikṣus long ago aroused the mind of the Great Vehicle,
but midway forgot this intent.
How can you instruct them with the Śrāvaka vehicle?
I observe that the wisdom of the Śrāvaka vehicle is shallow, like that of a blind person,
unable to discern the sharp or dull roots of all beings.'
Then Wéimójié entered samādhi,
enabling these bhikṣus to recollect their past lives,
where they had planted roots of virtue at the feet of five hundred Buddhas,
dedicating them to Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi.
Immediately, they regained their original minds with clarity.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus bowed at Wéimójié's feet.
At that time, Wéimójié expounded the Dharma for them,
and they never regressed from Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi.
I reflected that a Śrāvaka who does not observe others' roots should not expound the Dharma.
Therefore, I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
The Buddha said to Mahākātyāyana,
"You go visit Wéimójié and inquire about his illness."
Kātyāyana said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One,
I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
Why is this?
I recall once when the Buddha briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma to some bhikṣus,
I later elaborated on their meaning,
speaking on the meanings of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and extinction.
At that time, Wéimójié came and said to me,
'O Kātyāyana,
do not use a mind of arising and ceasing to speak of the Dharma of true reality.
Kātyāyana,
all dharmas ultimately neither arise nor cease—
this is the meaning of impermanence.
The five aggregates are thoroughly penetrated as empty and unarisen—
this is the meaning of suffering.
All dharmas are ultimately without existence—
this is the meaning of emptiness.
Self and non-self are non-dual—
this is the meaning of non-self.
Dharmas originally do not arise, and now do not cease—
this is the meaning of extinction.'
When he spoke this Dharma, those bhikṣus' minds attained liberation.
Therefore, I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
The Buddha said to Aniruddha,
"You go visit Wéimójié and inquire about his illness."
Aniruddha said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One,
I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
Why is this?
I recall once walking in meditation at a certain place,
when a Brahmā king named Yánjìng,
accompanied by ten thousand Brahmās, emitting pure light, came to where I was,
bowed, and asked me,
'What does Aniruddha see with his divine eye?'
I replied,
'Noble one,
I see this Śākyamuni Buddha's land of three thousand great thousand worlds,
as clearly as an āmalaka fruit in the palm of my hand.'
At that time, Wéimójié came and said to me,
'O Aniruddha,
does the divine eye perceive with constructed characteristics or without constructed characteristics?
If with constructed characteristics, it is no different from the five superknowledges of heterodox paths.
If without constructed characteristics, it is unconditioned and should not involve seeing.'
World-Honored One,
I was then silent.
Those Brahmās, hearing his words, attained what they had never had before,
and bowed to him, asking,
'Who in the world possesses the true divine eye?'
Wéimójié said,
'The Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses the true divine eye,
constantly abiding in samādhi, seeing all Buddha lands without dual characteristics.'
Thereupon, Brahmā King Yánjìng and his retinue of five hundred Brahmā devas
all aroused the mind of Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi.
After bowing at Wéimójié's feet, they suddenly vanished.
Therefore, I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
The Buddha said to Upāli,
"You go visit Wéimójié and inquire about his illness."
Upāli said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One,
I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
Why is this?
I recall that once there were two bhikṣus
who felt ashamed of having violated the precepts.
They dared not ask the Buddha,
so they came to me and said,
"O Upāli,
we have violated the precepts and are truly ashamed.
We dare not ask the Buddha.
We hope you can resolve our doubts and remorse so we may avoid this fault."
I then explained the Dharma to them accordingly.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me,
"O Upāli,
do not further increase the guilt of these two bhikṣus.
You should directly eliminate it and not disturb their minds.
Why is that?
The nature of their offense is not within, not without, and not in between.
As the Buddha has said,
'When the mind is defiled, beings are defiled;
when the mind is pure, beings are pure.'
The mind, too, is not within, not without, and not in between.
As the mind is so,
so are defilements and offenses.
So are all dharmas.
They do not depart from thusness.
O Upāli,
when you attained liberation through the characteristics of the mind,
was there any defilement?"
I replied,
"No."
Vimalakīrti said,
"The mind-nature of all beings is likewise without defilement.
O Upāli,
false thoughts are defilement; absence of false thoughts is purity.
Inverted views are defilement;
absence of inverted views is purity.
Clinging to self is defilement;
not clinging to self is purity.
Upāli,
all dharmas arise and cease without abiding,
like illusions, like lightning; dharmas do not depend on each other.
Not even for a single moment do they abide.
All dharmas are seen falsely,
like dreams, like mirages, like the moon in water, like images in a mirror—they arise from false thoughts.
One who understands this is called an upholder of the precepts.
One who understands this is called a skillful interpreter."
Then the two bhikṣus said,
"What supreme wisdom!
This is something Upāli cannot match.
Though foremost in upholding the precepts, he could not explain it thus."
I immediately replied,
"Apart from the Tathāgata, there is no śrāvaka or bodhisattva who can match his eloquence in discourse.
His wisdom and clarity are such as this."
At that time, the two bhikṣus' doubts and remorse were immediately removed.
They resolved to attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi
and made this vow:
"May all beings attain such eloquence."
Therefore, I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
The Buddha said to Rāhula,
"You go visit Vimalakīrti and inquire about his illness."
Rāhula said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One,
I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
Why is that?
I recall once when the sons of elders from Vaiśālī
came to me, bowed at my feet, and asked me,
'O Rāhula,
you are the Buddha's son.
You renounced the throne of a wheel-turning king to leave home and follow the Path.
What benefits are there in leaving home?'
I then explained to them according to the Dharma the benefits and merits of leaving home.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me,
'O Rāhula,
you should not speak of the benefits and merits of leaving home.
Why is that?
Having no benefit and no merit is true leaving home.
Conditioned dharmas may be said to have benefits and merits,
but leaving home is for the unconditioned.
In the unconditioned, there are no benefits and no merits.
Rāhula,
leaving home means no self, no other, and no in-between.
It means abiding in nirvāṇa, free from the sixty-two views.
It is what the wise accept and the noble practice.
It subdues the demons, liberates the five paths,
purifies the five eyes, attains the five powers, and establishes the five faculties.
It does not trouble others,
avoids all evils, and crushes heterodox views.
It transcends conventional names and emerges from the mire.
It is without attachment, without self-ownership,
without acceptance, without disturbance.
It harbors inner joy and protects others' minds.
It follows meditative concentration and avoids all faults.
If one can be like this, that is true leaving home.'
Then Vimalakīrti said to the elders' sons,
'You should all leave home together in the true Dharma.
Why is that?
It is difficult to encounter a Buddha in the world.'
The elders' sons said,
'Layman,
we have heard the Buddha say
that without parental permission, one cannot leave home.'
Vimalakīrti said,
'Indeed, but if you resolve to attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, that is leaving home.
That is complete fulfillment.'
At that time, thirty-two elders' sons
all resolved to attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"You go visit Vimalakīrti and inquire about his illness."
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One,
I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
Why is that?
I recall once when the World-Honored One had a slight illness and needed cow's milk.
I took my bowl and stood at the gate of a great brāhmaṇa's house.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me,
'O Ānanda,
why are you standing here with your bowl so early in the morning?'
I said,
'Layman,
the World-Honored One has a slight illness and needs cow's milk,
so I have come here.'
Vimalakīrti said,
'Enough, enough, Ānanda.
Do not speak such words.
The Tathāgata's body is a vajra body.
All evils have been cut off, all virtues universally gathered.
How could he have any illness or affliction?
Go quietly, Ānanda.
Do not slander the Tathāgata.
Do not let outsiders hear such coarse words,
nor let the mighty devas or bodhisattvas from other pure lands hear this.
Ānanda,
a wheel-turning sage king, with but little merit, remains free from illness;
how much more so the Tathāgata, who has immeasurable merit and universal supremacy?
Go, Ānanda,
do not make us suffer such shame.
If heterodox ascetics hear this, they will think,
"What kind of teacher is this?
He cannot even cure his own illness, yet he claims to cure others."
You should go quickly and secretly, and let no one hear.
You should know, Ānanda,
the bodies of all Tathāgatas are the Dharma-body, not a body of thought and desire.
The Buddha, as World-Honored One, transcends the three realms.
The Buddha's body is free from outflows; all outflows have been exhausted.
The Buddha's body is unconditioned and does not fall into any category.
Such a body—how could it have any illness or affliction?'
At that time, World-Honored One, I truly felt ashamed.
Could it be that I had heard incorrectly in the Buddha's presence?
Then I heard a voice from the sky saying,
'Ānanda,
it is as the layman says.
But because the Buddha appears in the world of five turbidities,
he manifests such methods to liberate beings.
Go, Ānanda,
take the milk without shame.'
World-Honored One,
Vimalakīrti's wisdom and eloquence are such as this.
Therefore, I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
Thus, five hundred great disciples
each related their past encounters to the Buddha,
recounting what Vimalakīrti had said,
and all declared they were not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
Then the Buddha said to Maitreya Bodhisattva,
"You go visit Vimalakīrti and inquire about his illness."
Maitreya said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One,
I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
Why is that?
I recall once when I was explaining the practice of the irreversible stage
to the God-king of Tuṣita and his retinue,
Vimalakīrti came and said to me,
'Maitreya,
the World-Honored One has predicted that you will attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi in one lifetime.
Upon which life did you receive this prediction?
A past life? A future life? Or the present life?
If a past life, it has already ceased.
If a future life, it has not yet come.
If the present life, the present life does not abide.
As the Buddha has said,
"Bhikṣu, at this very moment you are born, age, and cease."
If you received the prediction based on birthlessness,
birthlessness is the true position.
In the true position, there is no prediction,
nor attainment of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
How then, Maitreya, did you receive the prediction of one lifetime?
Did you receive it from the arising of thusness?
Or from the cessation of thusness?
If from the arising of thusness, thusness has no arising;
if from the cessation of thusness, thusness has no cessation.'
All sentient beings are thus.
All dharmas are also thus.
All sages and worthies are also thus.
Even Maitreya is thus.
If Maitreya receives a prediction,
then all sentient beings should also receive predictions.
Why is this?
Because 'thusness' is non-dual and undifferentiated.
If Maitreya attains Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi,
then all sentient beings should also attain it.
Why is this?
Because all sentient beings are precisely the mark of bodhi.
If Maitreya attains nirvāṇa,
then all sentient beings should also attain nirvāṇa.
Why is this?
Because all buddhas know that all sentient beings are ultimately tranquil and extinguished,
that is, the mark of nirvāṇa, with nothing further to extinguish.
Therefore, Maitreya,
do not use this dharma to tempt these heavenly beings.
Truly, there is no one who generates the mind of Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi,
nor is there anyone who regresses.
Maitreya, you should cause these heavenly beings to abandon their discriminating views of bodhi.
Why is this?
Bodhi
cannot be attained by the body,
nor can it be attained by the mind.
Tranquil extinction is bodhi, because it extinguishes all marks.
Non-observation is bodhi, because it transcends all conditions.
Non-action is bodhi, because it lacks recollection.
Severance is bodhi, because it abandons all views.
Detachment is bodhi, because it transcends all false thoughts.
Obstruction is bodhi, because it obstructs all aspirations.
Non-entry is bodhi, because it lacks attachment.
Accordance is bodhi, because it accords with thusness.
Abiding is bodhi, because it abides in the nature of dharmas.
Arrival is bodhi, because it reaches ultimate reality.
Non-duality is bodhi, because it transcends mental objects.
Equality is bodhi, because it equals emptiness.
The unconditioned is bodhi, because it lacks birth, abiding, and cessation.
Knowledge is bodhi, because it comprehends the mental activities of sentient beings.
Non-convergence is bodhi, because the sense bases do not converge.
Non-combination is bodhi, because it transcends habitual afflictions.
Non-location is bodhi, because it lacks form and color.
Provisional names are bodhi, because names are empty.
Like an illusion is bodhi, because it neither grasps nor rejects.
Without confusion is bodhi, because it is always naturally tranquil.
Well-tranquil is bodhi, because its nature is pure.
Non-grasping is bodhi, because it transcends clinging.
Without difference is bodhi, because all dharmas are equal.
Incomparable is bodhi, because there is nothing to compare it to.
Subtle is bodhi, because dharmas are difficult to know.
World-Honored One,
when Vimalakīrti spoke this dharma,
two hundred heavenly beings attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas.
Therefore, I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
The Buddha said to Guangyan Tongzi,
"You go visit Vimalakīrti and inquire about his illness."
Guangyan said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One,
I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
Why is this?
I recall once when I was leaving the great city of Vaiśālī,
Vimalakīrti was just entering the city.
I immediately bowed to him and asked,
'Layman, where have you come from?'
He replied to me,
'I have come from the place of enlightenment.'
I asked, 'What is the place of enlightenment?'
He answered,
'A straightforward mind is the place of enlightenment, because it is without falsity.
Practice is the place of enlightenment, because it accomplishes tasks.
A profound mind is the place of enlightenment, because it increases merit.
The bodhi mind is the place of enlightenment, because it is without error.
Giving is the place of enlightenment, because it expects no reward.
Precept observance is the place of enlightenment, because it fulfills vows.
Patience is the place of enlightenment, because it is unobstructed toward all sentient beings.
Diligence is the place of enlightenment, because it does not regress.
Meditation is the place of enlightenment, because it tames the mind.
Wisdom is the place of enlightenment, because it directly perceives all dharmas.
Kindness is the place of enlightenment, because it treats all sentient beings equally.
Compassion is the place of enlightenment, because it endures suffering.
Joy is the place of enlightenment, because it delights in the dharma.
Equanimity is the place of enlightenment, because it severs hatred and attachment.
Supernormal powers are the place of enlightenment, because they achieve the six penetrations.
Liberation is the place of enlightenment, because it can renounce.
Skillful means are the place of enlightenment, because they teach sentient beings.
The four means of attraction are the place of enlightenment, because they attract sentient beings.
Extensive learning is the place of enlightenment, because it practices what is heard.
Subduing the mind is the place of enlightenment, because it correctly contemplates all dharmas.
The thirty-seven aids to enlightenment are the place of enlightenment, because they renounce conditioned dharmas.
Truth is the place of enlightenment, because it does not deceive the world.
Dependent origination is the place of enlightenment, because ignorance up to old age and death are endless.
All afflictions are the place of enlightenment, because they are known as they truly are.
Sentient beings are the place of enlightenment, because they are known as selfless.
All dharmas are the place of enlightenment, because they are known as empty.
Subduing demons is the place of enlightenment, because it is unshakable.
The three realms are the place of enlightenment, because there is nowhere to go.
The lion's roar is the place of enlightenment, because it is fearless.
Powers, fearlessness, and unique dharmas are the place of enlightenment, because they are without faults.
The three insights are the place of enlightenment, because they have no remaining obstructions.
Knowing all dharmas in one thought is the place of enlightenment, because it accomplishes omniscience.
Thus, good man,
if a bodhisattva, in accordance with the pāramitās, teaches sentient beings,
then all actions, whether raising or lowering the foot,
should be known as coming from the place of enlightenment and abiding in the Buddha-dharma.'
When he spoke this dharma, five hundred heavenly beings generated the mind of Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness."
The Buddha said to the bodhisattva Chishi,
"You go visit Vimalakīrti and inquire about his illness."
Chishi said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One,
I am not qualified to visit him and inquire about his illness.
Why is this?
I recall once when I was dwelling in a quiet room,
Māra Pāpīyas, accompanied by twelve thousand heavenly maidens,
looking like Śakra, with music and singing, came to where I was.
Together with his retinue, he bowed at my feet,
joined his palms respectfully, and stood to one side.
I thought he was Śakra,
and said to him,
'Welcome, Kauśika.
Although you have merit, you should not be indulgent.
You should contemplate the impermanence of the five desires and seek the roots of goodness.
Cultivate the firm dharma regarding body, life, and wealth.'
He then said to me,
'Virtuous one,
accept these twelve thousand heavenly maidens to serve you.'
I said,
'Kauśika,
do not offer such improper things to me, a śramaṇa of the Śākya clan—this is not appropriate for me.'
Before I finished speaking, Vimalakīrti came and said to me,
'He is not Śakra;
he is Māra come to disturb you.'
He then said to Māra,
'You can give these maidens to me,
as I should accept them.'
Māra then became frightened, thinking,
'Vimalakīrti must not cause me trouble.'
He wanted to become invisible and leave but could not become invisible;
using all his supernatural power, he still could not leave.
Then a voice was heard in the sky saying,
'Pāpīyas,
give him the maidens, and then you can leave.'
Māra, out of fear, reluctantly gave them.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to the maidens,
'Māra has given you to me.
Now you should all generate the mind of Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.'
Then, according to their capacities, he taught them the dharma to generate the intention for enlightenment.
He further said,
'You have already generated the intention for enlightenment.
You have the joy of dharma to entertain yourselves;
you should no longer delight in the joy of the five desires.'
The heavenly maidens asked,
'What is the joy of dharma?'
He replied,
'Joy in constantly believing in the Buddha.
Joy in desiring to hear the dharma.
Joy in making offerings to the saṅgha.
Joy in renouncing the five desires.
Joy in contemplating the five aggregates as enemy thieves.
Joy in contemplating the four elements as poisonous snakes.
Joy in contemplating the internal sense bases as an empty village.
Joy in protecting the intention for enlightenment.
Joy in benefiting sentient beings.
Joy in revering and supporting teachers.
Joy in practicing giving extensively.
Joy in firmly upholding precepts.
Joy in patience and gentleness.
Joy in diligently accumulating roots of goodness.
Joy in meditation without distraction.
Joy in being free from defilements and having clear wisdom.
Joy in broadening the bodhi mind.
Joy in subduing all demons.
Joy in severing all afflictions.
Joy in purifying buddha-lands.
Joy in accomplishing the marks of excellence by cultivating all merits.
Joy in adorning the place of enlightenment.
Joy in hearing profound dharma without fear.
Joy in the three gates of liberation, not delighting in untimely things.
Joy in drawing near to fellow practitioners.
Joy in having no anger or obstruction toward those who are not fellow practitioners.
Joy in guiding and protecting bad friends.
Joy in drawing near to good friends.
Joy in a mind that delights in purity.
Joy in cultivating the immeasurable dharma of the aids to enlightenment.
This is the joy of dharma for bodhisattvas.'
Then Pāpīyas said to the maidens,
'I wish to return to the heavenly palace with you.'
The maidens said,
'You have given us to this layman.
We have the joy of dharma and are very happy;
we no longer delight in the joy of the five desires.'
Māra said,
'Layman, please release these maidens.
One who gives all one has to others
is a bodhisattva.'
Vímójié said:
"I have already renounced them.
You may take them away.
So that all living beings may attain fulfillment of the Dharma vows.
Thereupon, the women asked Vímójié:
"How are we to dwell in the demon palace?"
Vímójié said:
"Sisters, there is a Dharma gate called the Inexhaustible Lamp.
You should learn it.
The Inexhaustible Lamp means
just as one lamp can light hundreds and thousands of lamps,
so the darkness becomes bright,
and the light never ends.
Likewise, sisters,
when one bodhisattva guides hundreds of thousands of living beings,
causing them to develop the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi,
their intention for the Way does not diminish,
and through the teachings they expound, they themselves increase all wholesome dharmas.
This is called the Inexhaustible Lamp.
Although you dwell in the demon palace,
with this Inexhaustible Lamp,
you can cause countless devas and goddesses to develop the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This repays the Buddha's kindness
and greatly benefits all living beings."
At that time, the goddesses
bowed with their heads at Vímójié's feet
and followed the demon back to the palace, suddenly vanishing.
World-Honored One,
Vímójié possesses such sovereign spiritual powers, wisdom, and eloquence,
therefore I am not qualified to visit him to inquire about his illness."
The Buddha told the elder's son Shàndé:
"You go visit Vímójié to inquire about his illness."
Shàndé said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One,
I am not qualified to visit him to inquire about his illness.
Why?
I recall once holding a great almsgiving assembly at my father's house,
providing for all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, various outsiders, the poor, lowly, orphaned, and beggars,
lasting seven days.
Then Vímójié came into the assembly
and said to me:
'Elder's son,
a great almsgiving assembly should not be as you have set it up.
It should be a Dharma-giving assembly.
What is the use of this wealth-giving assembly?'
I said:
'Householder,
what is a Dharma-giving assembly?'
He replied:
'A Dharma-giving assembly
is one that simultaneously provides for all living beings, without before or after.
This is called a Dharma-giving assembly.'
I asked: 'What does that mean?'
He said: 'It means generating a mind of compassion through bodhi,
generating a mind of great compassion to save living beings,
generating a mind of joy by upholding the true Dharma,
practicing a mind of equanimity by gathering wisdom,
generating dāna-pāramitā by subduing miserliness,
generating śīla-pāramitā by transforming those who break precepts,
generating kṣānti-pāramitā through the Dharma of no-self,
generating vīrya-pāramitā by transcending body and mind phenomena,
generating dhyāna-pāramitā through the mark of bodhi,
generating prajñā-pāramitā through omniscience,
teaching living beings while abiding in emptiness,
not abandoning conditioned dharmas while abiding in signlessness,
showing rebirth while abiding in wishlessness,
protecting the true Dharma by employing skillful means,
saving living beings through the four means of attraction,
serving all respectfully to eliminate arrogance,
establishing the three steadfast practices regarding body, life, and wealth,
cultivating mindfulness in the six recollections,
developing a straightforward mind through the six harmonies,
practicing pure livelihood through right conduct of wholesome dharmas,
drawing near to sages and saints with a pure and joyful mind,
generating a tamed mind without hating evil people,
developing profound resolve through the monastic life,
increasing learning by practicing as taught,
dwelling in solitude through the Dharma of non-contention,
engaging in serene meditation while aspiring for Buddha-wisdom,
liberating beings from bonds through cultivated grounds,
accumulating merit by perfecting marks and purifying Buddha-lands,
engaging in wisdom by knowing all beings' thoughts and teaching accordingly,
knowing all dharmas without grasping or rejecting,
entering the single mark gate through wisdom,
cutting off all afflictions, obstacles, and unwholesome dharmas, engaging in all wholesome deeds to attain all wisdom and wholesome dharmas,
developing all dharmas that aid the Buddha-way.
Thus, good man,
this is the Dharma-giving assembly.
If a bodhisattva abides in such a Dharma-giving assembly,
they are a great benefactor,
and also a field of merit for all worlds.'
World-Honored One,
when Vímójié spoke this Dharma,
two hundred people among the brāhmaṇa assembly all developed the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, my mind became purified, and I sighed at this unprecedented event.
I bowed with my head at Vímójié's feet
and immediately took off my necklace worth hundreds of thousands,
offering it to him.
He would not accept it.
I said: 'Householder,
please accept it and use it as you wish.'
Vímójié then accepted the necklace and divided it into two parts.
He gave one part to the lowest beggar in the assembly
and offered the other part to the Buddha Nánshèng Rúlái.
The entire assembly saw the Buddha-land of Nánshèng Rúlái illuminated,
and also saw the pearl necklace on that Buddha transform into a four-pillared jeweled platform, adorned on all sides without obscuration.
Then Vímójié, having displayed this spiritual transformation, said:
'If a benefactor gives with equal mind to the lowest beggar,
it is like the field of merit of the Tathāgata, without discrimination,
equal in great compassion, not seeking reward.
This is called the fulfillment of Dharma-giving.'
The lowest beggar in the city,
seeing this spiritual power and hearing these words,
all developed the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, I am not qualified to visit him to inquire about his illness."
Thus, each bodhisattva told the Buddha their original circumstances,
relating what Vímójié had said,
and all declared they were not qualified to visit him to inquire about his illness.
Then the Buddha told Wénshū Shīlì:
"You go visit Vímójié to inquire about his illness."
Wénshū Shīlì said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One,
that superior one is difficult to match in response.
He profoundly realizes true reality and skillfully expounds the essentials of the Dharma.
His eloquence is unimpeded, his wisdom unhindered.
He fully knows all bodhisattva practices.
He enters all the secret treasuries of the Buddhas, subdues all demons, and sports with spiritual powers.
His wisdom and skillful means are all perfected.
Nevertheless, I will follow the Buddha's holy directive and visit him to inquire about his illness."
Thereupon, all the bodhisattvas, great disciples, gods, and four heavenly kings in the assembly thought:
"Now these two great beings, Wénshū Shīlì and Vímójié, will converse,
and surely expound wondrous Dharma."
Immediately, eight thousand bodhisattvas, five hundred śrāvakas,
and hundreds of thousands of devas and humans all wished to follow.
Thus, Wénshū Shīlì, surrounded respectfully by the bodhisattvas, great disciples, and devas and humans, entered the great city of Píyélí.
At that time, the elder Vímójié thought:
"Now Wénshū Shīlì is coming with the great assembly."
He immediately used his spiritual power to empty his room,
removing all contents and attendants,
leaving only a single couch on which he lay ill.
When Wénshū Shīlì entered his dwelling,
he saw the room empty, with nothing there, and him alone lying on a single couch.
Then Vímójié said:
"Welcome, Wénshū Shīlì.
You come without the mark of coming,
you see without the mark of seeing."
Wénshū Shīlì said:
"So it is, householder.
If one comes, they do not come again;
if one goes, they do not go again.
Why?
What comes has nowhere from which it comes; what goes has nowhere to which it goes; what is seen cannot be seen again.
But let us set this aside.
Householder,
is your illness tolerable?
Is the treatment reducing it, not increasing?
The World-Honored One sincerely inquires immeasurably.
Householder,
what is the cause of this illness?
How long has it existed?
How will it cease?"
Vímójié said:
"From ignorance comes attachment, hence my illness arises.
Because all living beings are ill, therefore I am ill.
If all living beings' illnesses cease, then my illness will cease.
Why?
The bodhisattva enters birth and death for the sake of living beings.
Where there is birth and death, there is illness.
If living beings are freed from illness,
then the bodhisattva will have no more illness.
Just as an elder with only one son falls ill when the son falls ill,
and recovers when the son recovers,
so too the bodhisattva
loves all living beings as his children.
When living beings are ill, the bodhisattva is ill;
when living beings recover, the bodhisattva recovers.
Moreover, you ask:
'What is the cause of this illness?'
The bodhisattva's illness arises from great compassion."
Wénshū Shīlì said:
"Householder,
why is this room empty, without attendants?"
Vímójié said:
"All Buddha-lands are likewise empty."
He asked again:
"With what is emptiness made empty?"
He replied:
"With emptiness, emptiness is made."
He asked again:
"Why empty emptiness?"
He replied:
"Because emptiness is without discrimination, it is empty."
He asked again:
"Can emptiness be discriminated?"
He replied:
"Discrimination is also empty."
He asked again:
"Where should emptiness be sought?"
He replied:
"It should be sought in the sixty-two views."
Another question was asked:
"Where should the sixty-two views be sought?"
The reply was:
"They should be sought within the liberation of all Buddhas."
Another question:
"Where should the liberation of all Buddhas be sought?"
The reply:
"It should be sought within the mental activities of all sentient beings."
"Also, why do you, benevolent one, have no attendants?"
"All demons and heretics are my attendants."
"Why is that?"
"Demons delight in birth and death,"
"While bodhisattvas do not abandon birth and death."
"Heretics delight in various views,"
"While bodhisattvas remain unmoved by various views."
Wénshū Shīlì said:
"Householder, what are the characteristics of your illness?"
Wéimójié replied:
"My illness is formless and cannot be seen."
Another question:
"Does this illness connect with the body or with the mind?"
The reply:
"Not with the body, because the body's form is separate;"
"Nor with the mind, because the mind is like an illusion."
Another question:
"Among the earth element, water element, fire element, and wind element,"
"Which element causes this illness?"
The reply:
"This illness is not of the earth element, yet not separate from it;"
"The same applies to water, fire, and wind elements."
"However, the illnesses of sentient beings arise from the four elements;"
"Because they are ill, therefore I am ill."
At that time, Wénshū Shīlì asked Wéimójié:
"How should a bodhisattva comfort and instruct an ill bodhisattva?"
Wéimójié said:
"Speak of the body's impermanence without advocating aversion to it;"
"Speak of the body's suffering without advocating delight in nirvana;"
"Speak of the body's selflessness while teaching and guiding sentient beings;"
"Speak of the body's emptiness without advocating complete extinction;"
"Speak of repenting past transgressions without dwelling on the past."
"Through one's own illness, have compassion for others' illnesses;"
"Recognize the suffering of countless past lifetimes;"
"Remember to benefit all sentient beings and recall accumulated merits;"
"Maintain pure livelihood;"
"Avoid worry and distress, always exert diligence;"
"Become a king of physicians to heal all illnesses."
"A bodhisattva should thus comfort and instruct an ill bodhisattva, bringing them joy."
Wénshū Shīlì said:
"Householder,"
"How does an ill bodhisattva tame their mind?"
Wéimójié replied:
"An ill bodhisattva should think thus:"
"My present illness arises from past delusions, inversions, and various afflictions;"
"There is no real entity that receives the illness."
"Why is that?"
"The combination of the four elements is provisionally called a body;"
"The four elements have no master, the body has no self."
"Moreover, this illness arises from attachment to self;"
"Therefore, one should not generate attachment to self."
"Knowing the root of illness, eliminate the notion of self and sentient beings;"
"Generate the notion of dharmas."
"Should think thus:"
"This body is merely composed of various dharmas;"
"Arises only as dharmas arise, ceases only as dharmas cease."
"Furthermore, these dharmas are unaware of each other;"
"When arising, they don't say 'I arise';"
"When ceasing, they don't say 'I cease.'"
"That ill bodhisattva, to eliminate the notion of dharmas,"
"Should think thus:"
"This notion of dharmas is also an inversion;"
"Inversion is a great affliction."
"I should depart from it."
"How to depart?"
"Depart from self and what belongs to self."
"How to depart from self and what belongs to self?"
"It means departing from dual dharmas."
"How to depart from dual dharmas?"
"It means not dwelling on internal and external dharmas, practicing equality."
"What is equality?"
"It is the equality of self and nirvana."
"Why is that?"
"Both self and nirvana are empty."
"In what sense are they empty?"
"They are empty because they are merely names."
"These two dharmas have no fixed nature."
"Attaining this equality, there are no other illnesses;"
"Only the illness of emptiness remains, and the illness of emptiness is also empty."
"This ill bodhisattva, through non-acceptance, accepts all acceptances;"
"Without fully possessing Buddha-dharma, does not extinguish acceptance to attain realization."
"If the body suffers, remember beings in miserable realms and generate great compassion;"
"Having tamed myself, I should tame all sentient beings;"
"Only eliminate their illnesses, not the dharmas;"
"Teach them to cut off the root of illness."
"What is the root of illness?"
"It is having objects of attachment."
"From having objects of attachment arises the root of illness."
"What are the objects of attachment? They are the three realms."
"How to cut off attachment? Through non-attainment."
"If there is non-attainment, there is no attachment."
"What is non-attainment?"
"It means departing from two views."
"What are the two views?"
"Internal view and external view—this is non-attainment."
"Wénshū Shīlì,"
"This is how an ill bodhisattva tames their mind."
"To end the suffering of aging, sickness, and death is the bodhisattva's enlightenment."
"If not thus, one's practice lacks wise benefit."
"For example, only overcoming enemies constitutes courage;"
"Similarly, simultaneously eliminating aging, sickness, and death defines a bodhisattva."
"That ill bodhisattva should further think thus:"
"As my illness is neither real nor existent,"
"So too the illnesses of sentient beings are neither real nor existent."
"When contemplating thus,"
"If toward sentient beings one generates love-view great compassion,"
"It should be abandoned."
"Why is that?"
"Bodhisattvas eliminate adventitious defilements and generate great compassion;"
"Love-view compassion produces weariness with birth and death."
"If able to depart from this, there is no weariness;"
"In all rebirths, one is not covered by love-views."
"Unbound in rebirth, one can teach sentient beings to unbind."
"As the Buddha said:"
"If bound oneself, to unbind others—this is impossible;"
"If unbound oneself,"
"To unbind others—this is possible."
"Therefore, a bodhisattva should not generate bondage."
"What is bondage? What is liberation?"
"Craving meditative bliss is a bodhisattva's bondage;"
"Arising through skillful means is a bodhisattva's liberation."
"Also, wisdom without skillful means is bondage;"
"Wisdom with skillful means is liberation."
"Skillful means without wisdom is bondage;"
"Skillful means with wisdom is liberation."
"What is wisdom without skillful means bondage?"
"It means a bodhisattva with love-view mind,"
"Adorns Buddha-lands and matures sentient beings,"
"While personally practicing emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;"
"This is called wisdom without skillful means bondage."
"What is wisdom with skillful means liberation?"
"It means not using love-view mind to adorn Buddha-lands or mature sentient beings,"
"In emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness,"
"Personally practicing without weariness;"
"This is called wisdom with skillful means liberation."
"What is skillful means without wisdom bondage?"
"It means a bodhisattva abiding in greed, anger, wrong views, and other afflictions,"
"Yet planting roots of virtue;"
"This is called skillful means without wisdom bondage."
"What is skillful means with wisdom liberation?"
"It means departing from greed, anger, wrong views, and other afflictions,"
"Planting roots of virtue,"
"And dedicating them to Anòuduōluó Sānmiǎosānpútí;"
"This is called skillful means with wisdom liberation."
"Wénshū Shīlì,"
"That ill bodhisattva should thus contemplate all dharmas."
"Also, contemplate the body as impermanent, suffering, empty, and selfless;"
"This is called wisdom."
"Though the body is ill, always remain in birth and death,"
"Benefiting all without weariness;"
"This is called skillful means."
"Also, contemplate the body: body not separate from illness, illness not separate from body;"
"This illness, this body, neither new nor old;"
"This is called wisdom."
"Though the body is ill, not eternally extinguishing;"
"This is called skillful means."
"Wénshū Shīlì,"
"An ill bodhisattva should thus tame their mind without dwelling in it,"
"Nor dwelling in an untamed mind."
"Why is that?"
"Dwelling in an untamed mind is the way of fools;"
"Dwelling in a tamed mind is the way of śrāvakas."
"Therefore, a bodhisattva should not dwell in tamed or untamed mind;"
"Departing from these two dharmas is bodhisattva conduct."
"Abiding in birth and death without defiled actions;"
"This is bodhisattva conduct."
"Not ordinary person's conduct, not sage's conduct;"
"This is bodhisattva conduct."
"Not defiled conduct, not pure conduct;"
"This is bodhisattva conduct."
"Though transcending demonic conduct,"
"Manifests subduing all demons;"
"This is bodhisattva conduct."
"Seeking all wisdom without untimely seeking;"
"This is bodhisattva conduct."
"Though contemplating all dharmas as unproduced, not entering the true position;"
"This is bodhisattva conduct."
"Though contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, enters all wrong views;"
"This is bodhisattva conduct."
"Though gathering all sentient beings, without attachment;"
"This is bodhisattva conduct."
"Though delighting in detachment, not relying on exhaustion of body and mind;"
"This is bodhisattva conduct."
"Though acting in the three realms, not destroying Dharma-nature;"
"This is bodhisattva conduct."
"Though practicing emptiness, planting roots of virtue;"
"This is bodhisattva conduct."
"Though practicing signlessness, liberating sentient beings;"
"This is bodhisattva conduct."
"Though practicing wishlessness, manifesting receiving a body;"
"This is bodhisattva conduct."
Although practicing non-arising, yet giving rise to all virtuous practices.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although practicing the six pāramitās, yet fully understanding the minds and mental factors of all beings.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although practicing the six supernatural powers, yet not exhausting the contaminants.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although practicing the four immeasurable minds, yet not craving rebirth in the Brahma world.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although practicing meditation, liberation, and samādhi, yet not following rebirth through meditation.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although practicing the four foundations of mindfulness, yet not permanently abandoning body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although practicing the four right efforts, yet not relinquishing physical and mental vigor.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although practicing the four bases of spiritual power, yet attaining mastery and supernatural abilities.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although practicing the five faculties, yet discerning the sharp and dull faculties of beings.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although practicing the five powers, yet delighting in seeking the ten powers of a buddha.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although practicing the seven factors of enlightenment, yet discerning the wisdom of a buddha.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although practicing the noble eightfold path, yet delighting in practicing the immeasurable buddha path.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although practicing the methods of calming and insight as aids to the path, yet not ultimately falling into extinction.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although practicing the non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena, yet adorning the body with marks and beauties.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although displaying the demeanor of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, yet not abandoning the buddhadharma.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although following the ultimate pure nature of all phenomena, yet manifesting the body according to what is appropriate.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although observing all buddha lands as eternally still like space, yet manifesting various pure buddha lands.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although attaining buddhahood, turning the wheel of dharma, and entering nirvāṇa, yet not abandoning the bodhisattva path.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
When these words were spoken, in the great assembly led by Wénshūshīlì,
