eight thousand gods among them all generated the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Shèlìfú,
seeing that there were no seats in the room,
thought thus:
"Where will all these bodhisattvas and great disciples sit?"
The elder Wéimójié knew his thought
and said to Shèlìfú:
"What is it, Venerable?
Have you come for the dharma or for a seat?"
Shèlìfú said:
"I have come for the dharma, not for a seat."
Wéimójié said:
"O Shèlìfú,
those who seek the dharma do not covet their bodies or lives,
let alone seats.
Those who seek the dharma
do not seek form, sensation, perception, formations, or consciousness.
They do not seek the realms or entrances.
They do not seek the desire realm, form realm, or formless realm.
O Shèlìfú,
those who seek the dharma
do not cling to seeking the buddha, do not cling to seeking the dharma, do not cling to seeking the saṅgha.
Those who seek the dharma
do not seek to see suffering, do not seek to eradicate origination,
do not seek to realize cessation or cultivate the path.
Why is that?
The dharma is beyond conceptualization.
If one says, 'I shall see suffering, eradicate origination, realize cessation, and cultivate the path,'
that is conceptualization, not seeking the dharma.
O Shèlìfú,
the dharma is called cessation.
If one practices arising and cessation, that is seeking arising and cessation, not seeking the dharma.
The dharma is called undefiled.
If one is defiled by the dharma, even up to nirvāṇa,
that is defilement, not seeking the dharma.
The dharma has no place of practice.
If one practices in the dharma, that is having a place of practice, not seeking the dharma.
The dharma is beyond grasping and rejecting.
If one grasps or rejects the dharma, that is grasping and rejecting, not seeking the dharma.
The dharma has no location.
If one clings to a location,
that is clinging to a location, not seeking the dharma.
The dharma is called formless.
If one follows forms and cognition, that is seeking forms, not seeking the dharma.
The dharma cannot be abided in.
If one abides in the dharma, that is abiding in the dharma, not seeking the dharma.
The dharma cannot be seen, heard, sensed, or known.
If one practices seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing,
that is seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, not seeking the dharma.
The dharma is called unconditioned.
If one practices the conditioned, that is seeking the conditioned, not seeking the dharma.
Therefore, Shèlìfú,
if one seeks the dharma,
one should seek nothing in all dharmas."
When these words were spoken,
five hundred gods attained the pure dharma eye in all dharmas.
Then the elder Wéimójié asked Wénshūshīlì:
"Venerable,
you have traveled through immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya lands.
In which buddha land are there excellent, sublime, meritorious lion seats?"
Wénshūshīlì said:
"Householder,
eastward, beyond thirty-six gaṅgā-nadī-vālukā lands, there is a world
named Xūmí Xiàng.
Its buddha is called Xūmí Dēng Wáng.
He is presently present.
That buddha's body is eighty-four thousand yojanas tall.
His lion seats are eighty-four thousand yojanas high, most excellently adorned."
Thereupon the elder Wéimójié,
manifesting his supernatural power,
immediately caused that buddha to send thirty-two thousand lion seats, high, broad, and splendidly pure,
to enter Wéimójié's room.
The bodhisattvas, great disciples, Śakras, Brahmās, and the four heavenly kings had never seen such before.
The room became vast and spacious, entirely accommodating the thirty-two thousand lion seats
without any obstruction.
The city of Píyélí, as well as Jambudvīpa and the four continents,
were also not cramped,
appearing as before.
Then Wéimójié said to Wénshūshīlì:
"Take the lion seats.
Sit together with all the bodhisattvas and exalted ones.
You should make your bodies like those seats."
Those bodhisattvas who had attained supernatural powers transformed themselves
to be forty-two thousand yojanas tall and sat on the lion seats.
But the newly resolved bodhisattvas and great disciples could not ascend.
Then Wéimójié said to Shèlìfú:
"Take a lion seat."
Shèlìfú said:
"Householder,
these seats are too high and broad; I cannot ascend."
Wéimójié said:
"O Shèlìfú,
pay homage to the Tathāgata Xūmí Dēng Wáng, and then you may sit."
Thereupon the newly resolved bodhisattvas and great disciples
paid homage to the Tathāgata Xūmí Dēng Wáng
and were then able to sit on the lion seats.
Shèlìfú said:
"Householder, this is unprecedented!
Such a small room can accommodate these high and broad seats
without obstructing the city of Píyélí,
and also without cramping the villages, towns, and cities of Jambudvīpa, or the palaces of the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and spirits throughout the four continents."
Wéimójié said:
"O Shèlìfú,
the buddhas and bodhisattvas have a liberation called inconceivable.
If a bodhisattva abides in this liberation,
they can place the height and breadth of Mount Sumeru inside a mustard seed without increasing or decreasing it.
The original form of Mount Sumeru remains as before,
and the four heavenly kings and Trāyastriṃśa gods
are unaware of entering it.
Only those who should be liberated see Mount Sumeru entering the mustard seed.
This is called abiding in the gate of the inconceivable liberation dharma.
Moreover, they can place the waters of the four great oceans into a single pore
without disturbing the fish, turtles, sea turtles, and other water-dwelling creatures.
The original form of the great ocean remains as before,
and the nāgas, spirits, and asuras are unaware of entering it.
The beings are also undisturbed.
Moreover, Shèlìfú,
a bodhisattva abiding in the inconceivable liberation
can cut off and take a trichiliocosm
like a potter's wheel and place it in the palm of the right hand,
then toss it beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Gaṅgā River.
The beings within are unaware of going anywhere.
Then it is returned to its original place,
without anyone having the thought of coming or going.
The original form of this world remains as before.
Moreover, Shèlìfú,
if there are beings who delight in long abiding in the world and can be liberated,
the bodhisattva extends seven days into a kalpa,
causing those beings to perceive it as a kalpa.
If there are beings who do not delight in long abiding and can be liberated,
the bodhisattva compresses a kalpa into seven days,
causing those beings to perceive it as seven days.
Moreover, Shèlìfú,
a bodhisattva abiding in the inconceivable liberation
gathers all the adornments of all buddha lands
into a single land to show beings.
Moreover, a bodhisattva places all the beings of one buddha land in the right palm
and flies to the ten directions, showing them to all,
without moving from the original spot.
Moreover, Shèlìfú, the offerings made by beings in the ten directions to all buddhas—a bodhisattva can make them all visible in a single pore.
Moreover, all the suns, moons, and stars in the lands of the ten directions—a bodhisattva can make them all visible in a single pore.
Moreover, Shèlìfú,
all the winds in the worlds of the ten directions—a bodhisattva can inhale them into the mouth without harm to the body,
and the external trees are not broken.
Moreover, when the kalpas of the worlds in the ten directions end in conflagration,
a bodhisattva can take all the fires into the abdomen,
the fire continues as before without causing harm.
Moreover, below, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Gaṅgā River,
a bodhisattva can take one buddha land
and lift it upward, beyond countless worlds as numerous as the sands of the Gaṅgā River,
like holding a needle tip to lift a jujube leaf without disturbance.
Moreover, Shèlìfú,
a bodhisattva abiding in the inconceivable liberation
can manifest through supernatural power as a buddha body,
or manifest as a pratyekabuddha body,
or manifest as a śrāvaka body,
or manifest as the body of Śakra,
or manifest as the body of a Brahmā king,
or manifest as the body of a world ruler,
or manifest as the body of a cakravartin king."
Moreover, all sounds in the ten directions' worlds,
whether high, medium, or low tones, can be transformed to become the Buddha's voice,
performing the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness.
And the various teachings spoken by all Buddhas of the ten directions,
all of these
are universally made audible.
Śāriputra,
I now briefly describe the bodhisattva's inconceivable liberation power.
If explained extensively, an eon would not exhaust it.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa,
hearing this teaching of the bodhisattva's inconceivable liberation,
marveled at what he had never heard before,
and said to Śāriputra:
It is like someone displaying various colors before a blind person—they cannot see them.
All śrāvakas hearing this inconceivable liberation teaching
are similarly unable to comprehend it.
When the wise hear this,
who would not develop anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi mind?
Why should we permanently sever our roots,
being like spoiled seeds in this Mahāyāna?
All śrāvakas hearing this inconceivable liberation teaching
should weep and wail, their voices shaking the three-thousand-great-thousand worlds.
All bodhisattvas should greatly rejoice and receive this teaching with reverence.
If there are bodhisattvas who believe and understand the inconceivable liberation teaching,
all demon hosts cannot do anything to them.
When Mahākāśyapa spoke these words,
thirty-two thousand devas all developed anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi mind.
Then Vimalakīrti said to Mahākāśyapa:
Virtuous one,
among the countless asaṃkhyeya worlds in the ten directions, those who become demon kings
are mostly bodhisattvas abiding in inconceivable liberation,
who through skillful means teach sentient beings by appearing as demon kings.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
countless bodhisattvas in the ten directions

may have people begging for their hands, feet, ears, nose, head, eyes, marrow, brain, blood, flesh, skin, bones, villages, cities, wife, children, slaves, elephants, horses, carriages, gold, silver, vaidūrya, mother-of-pearl, carnelian, coral, amber, pearls, cowrie shells, clothing, food, and drink.
Those who beg thus are mostly bodhisattvas abiding in inconceivable liberation,
who through skillful means test them to make them firm.
Why is this?
Bodhisattvas abiding in inconceivable liberation
possess majestic virtue and power, thus they manifest oppressive actions,
showing sentient beings such difficult practices.
Ordinary people of inferior capacity lack the power
to thus oppress bodhisattvas.
It is like an elephant's trampling that a donkey cannot endure.
This is called the wisdom and skillful means gate of bodhisattvas abiding in inconceivable liberation.
Then Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti:
How does a bodhisattva regard sentient beings?
Vimalakīrti said:
Like a magician viewing the person he conjures,
thus does a bodhisattva regard sentient beings.
Like a wise person seeing the moon in water,
like seeing one's face in a mirror,
like flames in the heat,
like the echo of a voice,
like clouds in the sky,
like foam on water,
like bubbles on water,
like the firmness of a plantain tree,
like the lasting of lightning,
like a fifth great element,
like a sixth aggregate,
like a seventh sense faculty,
like a thirteenth sense base,
like a nineteenth realm,
thus does a bodhisattva regard sentient beings.
Like form in the formless realm,
like a scorched seed sprouting,
like a stream-enterer's view of self,
like a non-returner entering the womb,
like an arhat's three poisons,
like a patience-attaining bodhisattva's greed, anger, and moral transgressions,
like a Buddha's habit energy of afflictions,
like a blind person seeing forms,
like one in cessation samādhi having inhalation and exhalation,
like bird tracks in the sky,
like the son of a barren woman,
like a conjured person having afflictions,
like what is seen in a dream after awakening,
like an extinguished one receiving a body,
like a fire without smoke,
thus does a bodhisattva regard sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī said:
If a bodhisattva contemplates thus,
how does they practice compassion?
Vimalakīrti said:
After contemplating thus, the bodhisattva reflects:
I should speak such Dharma to sentient beings.
This is true compassion.
Practice nirvāṇa-compassion, for nothing is born.
Practice non-heating compassion, for there are no afflictions.
Practice equal compassion, for it equalizes the three times.
Practice non-contention compassion, for nothing arises.
Practice non-dual compassion, for internal and external do not combine; practice indestructible compassion, for it ultimately ends.
Practice firm compassion, for the mind is undamaged.
Practice pure compassion, for the nature of all dharmas is pure.
Practice boundless compassion, like space.
Practice arhat compassion, for it destroys the bandits of fetters.
Practice bodhisattva compassion, for it comforts sentient beings.
Practice Tathāgata compassion, for it attains suchness.
Practice Buddha compassion, for it awakens sentient beings.
Practice natural compassion, for it is attained without cause.
Practice bodhi compassion, for it is of one taste.
Practice unequaled compassion, for it severs all craving.
Practice great pity compassion, for it guides with Mahāyāna.
Practice tireless compassion, for it contemplates emptiness and selflessness.
Practice Dharma-giving compassion, for it gives without regret.
Practice moral precept compassion, for it transforms moral transgressors.
Practice patience compassion, for it protects self and others.
Practice diligence compassion, for it bears the burden of sentient beings.
Practice meditation compassion, for it does not cling to flavors.
Practice wisdom compassion, for it knows all at the proper time.
Practice skillful means compassion, for it manifests in all things.
Practice unhidden compassion, for the straightforward mind is pure.
Practice profound mind compassion, for it is unmixed with other practices.
Practice undeceiving compassion, for it is not false.
Practice peace and bliss compassion, for it enables attainment of Buddha's bliss.
Such is the bodhisattva's compassion.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
What is called pity?
He replied:
The merits cultivated by the bodhisattva
are all shared with all sentient beings.
What is called joy?
He replied:
When benefiting others, rejoice without regret.
What is called equanimity?
He replied:
Cultivating blessings without any expectation.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
For the fear in birth and death, what should the bodhisattva rely on?
Vimalakīrti said:
In the fear of birth and death,
the bodhisattva should rely on the Tathāgata's merit power.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
If the bodhisattva wishes to rely on the Tathāgata's merit power,
where should they abide?
He replied:
The bodhisattva wishing to rely on the Tathāgata's merit power
should abide in liberating all sentient beings.
He asked again:
Wishing to liberate sentient beings, what should be eliminated?
He replied:
Wishing to liberate sentient beings, eliminate their afflictions.
He asked again:
Wishing to eliminate afflictions, what should be practiced?
He replied:
Practice right mindfulness.
He asked again:
How does one practice right mindfulness?
He replied:
Practice non-arising and non-ceasing.
He asked again:
What dharma does not arise? What dharma does not cease?
He replied:
Unwholesome dharmas do not arise; wholesome dharmas do not cease.
He asked again:
What is the root of wholesome and unwholesome?
He replied: The body is the root.
He asked again:
What is the root of the body?
He replied:
Desire and craving are the root.
He asked again:
What is the root of desire and craving?
He replied:
False discrimination is the root.
He asked again:
What is the root of false discrimination?
He replied:
Inverted thoughts are the root.
He asked again:
What is the root of inverted thoughts?
He replied:
Non-abiding is the root.
He asked again:
What is the root of non-abiding?
He replied:
Non-abiding has no root.
Mañjuśrī,
from the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established.
At that time, in Vimalakīrti's room was a celestial maiden
who, seeing the great ones hearing the spoken Dharma, manifested her form
and scattered celestial flowers over the bodhisattvas and great disciples.
The flowers falling on the bodhisattvas all dropped off,
but those falling on the great disciples stuck and did not fall.
All the disciples used their spiritual power to remove the flowers but could not make them go away.
Then the celestial maiden asked Śāriputra:
Why are you removing the flowers?
He replied:
These flowers are not in accord with Dharma, thus I remove them. The celestial said:
Do not say these flowers are not in accord with Dharma.
Why?
These flowers make no discrimination.
You yourself generate discriminatory thoughts.
If leaving home in the Buddha's Dharma involves discrimination, that is not in accord with Dharma.
If there is no discrimination, that is in accord with Dharma.
Observing that the flowers do not stick to the bodhisattvas—they have already severed all discriminatory thoughts.
For instance, when a person is fearful, non-humans take advantage of them.
Similarly, because disciples fear birth and death,
forms, sounds, scents, tastes, and touches take advantage of them.
For those who have already transcended fear, all five desires are powerless.
When habitual afflictions are not yet exhausted, flowers cling to the body;
when habitual afflictions are exhausted, flowers do not cling.
Śāriputra said,
"Heavenly being, how long have you been dwelling in this room?"
She replied,
"I have dwelled here as long as you, Elder, have attained liberation."
Śāriputra said,
"Have you dwelled here that long?"
The heavenly being said,
"And how long has the Elder's liberation been?"
Śāriputra remained silent and did not answer.
The heavenly being said,
"Why does an elder of great wisdom remain silent?"
He replied,
"Liberation is beyond verbal expression, so I do not know what to say."
The heavenly being said,
"Words and letters are all marks of liberation.
Why is that?
Liberation is not within, not without, and not in between.
Words and letters are also not within, not without, and not in between.
Therefore, Śāriputra,
do not speak of liberation apart from words and letters.
Why is that?
All dharmas are marks of liberation."
Śāriputra said,
"Is it not said that liberation means freedom from desire, anger, and ignorance?"
The heavenly being said,
"The Buddha taught those with overweening pride
that liberation means freedom from desire, anger, and ignorance.
But for those without overweening pride,
the Buddha taught that the nature of desire, anger, and ignorance is itself liberation."
Śāriputra said,
"Excellent, excellent!
Heavenly maiden,
what have you attained, and what realization do you have, that your eloquence is like this?"
The heavenly being said,
"It is precisely because I have no attainment and no realization that my eloquence is thus.
Why is that?
If one has attainment and realization, they are considered to have overweening pride in the Buddha's Dharma."
Śāriputra asked the heavenly being,
"Among the three vehicles, which do you aspire to?"
The heavenly being said,
"When I teach beings through the Śrāvaka Dharma, I am a Śrāvaka;
when I teach beings through the Pratyekabuddha Dharma, I am a Pratyekabuddha;
when I teach beings through the Mahāyāna Dharma of great compassion, I am a Mahāyānist.
Śāriputra,
just as one who enters a garden of champaka flowers smells only champaka and no other scent,
so too, whoever enters this room
hears only the fragrance of the Buddha's merits,
and does not delight in the fragrance of Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha merits.
Śāriputra,
when Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, gods, dragons, spirits, and others enter this room,
hearing this noble one expound the true Dharma,
they all delight in the fragrance of the Buddha's merits and depart with awakened minds.
Śāriputra,
I have dwelled in this room for twelve years,
and never once have I heard teachings on the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha Dharma,
but only the inconceivable Dharma of the great compassion of bodhisattvas and the Buddhas.
Śāriputra,
this room constantly manifests eight rare and unprecedented dharmas.
What are these eight?
This room is always illuminated by a golden light, day and night without difference,
not relying on the sun or moon for illumination.
This is the first rare and unprecedented dharma.
Those who enter this room are not troubled by any defilements.
This is the second rare and unprecedented dharma.
This room constantly hosts visits from Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and bodhisattvas from other realms without interruption.
This is the third rare and unprecedented dharma.
This room constantly teaches the six pāramitās and the dharma of non-retrogression.
This is the fourth rare and unprecedented dharma.
This room always produces the foremost heavenly music, with strings emitting immeasurable sounds of Dharma transformation.
This is the fifth rare and unprecedented dharma.
This room contains four great treasuries filled with abundant jewels,
providing for the poor and needy endlessly.
This is the sixth rare and unprecedented dharma.
In this room, Śākyamuni Buddha,
Āmítuó Fó,
Āchù Fó,
Bǎo Dé,
Bǎo Yán,
Bǎo Yuè,
Bǎo Yán,
Nán Shèng,
Shīzi Xiǎng,
Yīqiè Lì Chéng,
and countless other Buddhas from the ten directions—
when this noble one brings them to mind,
they all come to extensively expound the secret essentials of the Buddhas' Dharma treasuries, and after speaking, they depart.
This is the seventh rare and unprecedented dharma.
In this room, all the adorned palaces of the heavens and the pure lands of the Buddhas are manifested.
This is the eighth rare and unprecedented dharma.
Śāriputra,
this room constantly manifests these eight rare and unprecedented dharmas.
Who, having witnessed such inconceivable matters,
would still delight in the Śrāvaka Dharma?"
Śāriputra said,
"Why do you not transform your female body?"
The heavenly being said,
"For twelve years, I have sought the characteristic of a female,
but ultimately found it unobtainable.
What is there to transform?
It is like a magician creating an illusory woman—
if someone were to ask why she does not transform her female body,
would that be a proper question?"
Śāriputra said,
"No,
for an illusion has no fixed characteristic; what is there to transform?"
The heavenly being said, "All dharmas are likewise, without fixed characteristics.
Why then ask about not transforming a female body?"
Immediately, the heavenly maiden, using her supernatural power,
transformed Śāriputra to appear like a heavenly maiden,
while she herself transformed to appear like Śāriputra.
She then asked,
"Why do you not transform your female body?"
Śāriputra, in the form of a heavenly maiden, replied,
"I do not know how I have transformed into a female body."
The heavenly being said,
"Śāriputra,
if you could transform this female body,
then all women should be able to transform as well.
Just as Śāriputra, though not a woman, appears in a female form,
so too are all women—
though appearing in female forms, they are not truly female.
Therefore, the Buddha said all dharmas are neither male nor female."
Immediately, the heavenly maiden withdrew her supernatural power,
and Śāriputra's body returned to its original form.
The heavenly being asked Śāriputra,
"Where has the form and characteristic of the female body gone now?"
Śāriputra said,
"The form and characteristic of the female body are neither here nor there."
The heavenly being said,
"All dharmas are likewise—
neither here nor there.
This 'neither here nor there' is what the Buddha taught."
Śāriputra asked the heavenly being,
"Where will you be reborn after you pass away here?"
The heavenly being said,
"I will be born as the Buddha's transformations are born."
Śāriputra said, "The Buddha's transformations are not born through death and rebirth."
The heavenly being said,
"So too are sentient beings—there is no death and rebirth."
Śāriputra asked the heavenly being,
"How long until you attain Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi?"
The heavenly being said,
"When you, Śāriputra, return to being an ordinary person,
then I will attain Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi."
Śāriputra said,
"It is impossible for me to become an ordinary person again."
The heavenly being said,
"It is likewise impossible for me to attain Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi.
Why is that?
Because bodhi has no abode,
thus there is no one who attains it."
Śāriputra said,
"But the Buddhas who have attained, are attaining, and will attain Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi—
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—
what does that mean?"
The heavenly being said,
"That is spoken through conventional words and numbers,
referring to the three periods of time,
not meaning that bodhi has past, future, or present."
The heavenly being said,
"Śāriputra,
have you attained the path of an Arhat?"
He said, "It is through no attainment that I have attained."
The heavenly being said,
"So too with all Buddhas and bodhisattvas—
it is through no attainment that they attain."
Then Vimalakīrti
said to Śāriputra,
"This heavenly maiden has already made offerings to ninety-two billion Buddhas,
can play with bodhisattva supernatural powers,
has fulfilled her vows, attained the patient acceptance of non-arising, and abides in non-retrogression.
Due to her original vows, she can manifest at will to teach and transform beings."
Then Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti,
"How does a bodhisattva penetrate the Buddha's path?"
Vimalakīrti said,
"If a bodhisattva practices the non-path,
that is penetrating the Buddha's path."
Mañjuśrī asked again,
"How does a bodhisattva practice the non-path?"
Vimalakīrti replied,
"If a bodhisattva practices the five heinous crimes without anger or hatred,
enters hell without any sinful defilements,
enters the animal realm without ignorance, arrogance, or other faults,
enters the hungry ghost realm while possessing full merits,
practices the paths of the form and formless realms without considering them superior,
manifests greed while free from all attachments,
manifests anger while harboring no enmity or obstruction toward beings,
manifests ignorance while using wisdom to tame the mind."
He manifests the practice of miserliness yet relinquishes all internal and external possessions without begrudging body or life.
He manifests the practice of breaking precepts yet abides securely in pure discipline.
Even regarding minor offenses, he still harbors great dread.
He manifests the practice of anger yet constantly maintains compassion and patience.
He manifests the practice of indolence yet diligently cultivates merit.
He manifests the practice of distracted mind yet constantly recollects concentration.
He manifests the practice of ignorance yet penetrates the wisdom of both worldly and transcendent realms.
He manifests the practice of deceit yet skillfully employs expedient means in accordance with the meanings of the scriptures.
He manifests the practice of arrogance yet serves as a bridge for all beings.
He manifests all afflictions yet his mind is ever pure.
He enters the realm of demons yet conforms to Buddha's wisdom, not following other teachings.
He enters the state of Śrāvaka yet expounds to beings the Dharma they have not heard.
He enters the state of Pratyekabuddha yet accomplishes great compassion to teach and transform beings.
He enters poverty yet possesses the treasure-hand with inexhaustible merits.
He enters physical mutilation yet is endowed with all marks of excellence to adorn himself.
He enters lowly status yet is born in the Buddha lineage, possessing all merits.
He enters frailty and ugliness yet attains a Nārāyaṇa body.
Which all beings delight to see.
He enters old age and sickness yet eternally severs the root of illness, transcending the fear of death.
He manifests having livelihood resources yet constantly contemplates impermanence, truly having no greed.
He manifests having wives, concubines, and maidens yet constantly remains far from the mire of the five desires.
He appears dull and slow yet accomplishes eloquence and retains all teachings without loss.
He enters heterodox salvations yet uses the right salvation to liberate all beings.
He appears to enter all paths yet cuts off their causes and conditions.
He manifests nirvana yet does not sever birth and death.
Mañjuśrī,
when a Bodhisattva can practice in such non-paths,
this is called penetrating the Buddha Way.
Then Vimalakīrti asked Mañjuśrī,
"What constitutes the Tathāgata seed?"
Mañjuśrī said,
"The body is the seed.
Ignorance and craving are the seed.
Greed, anger, and delusion are the seed.
The four perverted views are the seed.
The five hindrances are the seed.
The six sense bases are the seed.
The seven stations of consciousness are the seed.
The eight wrong paths are the seed.
The nine sources of annoyance are the seed.
The ten unwholesome paths are the seed.
In essence,
the sixty-two views and all afflictions are Buddha seeds.
Vimalakīrti asked, "What does this mean?"
He answered,
"If one sees the unconditioned and enters the right position,
one cannot again generate the mind of Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi.
For example, on high plateaus and dry land, lotuses do not grow; it is in low, muddy wetlands that these flowers bloom.
Similarly, those who see the unconditioned Dharma and enter the right position
can never again give rise to the Buddha Dharma.
It is in the mud of afflictions that beings can generate the Buddha Dharma.
Again, like sowing seeds in empty space, they ultimately cannot grow,
while in manure-rich soil they can flourish.
Thus, those who enter the unconditioned right position do not generate the Buddha Dharma.
But those with self-view as huge as Mount Sumeru
can still generate the mind of Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi and produce the Buddha Dharma.
Therefore, know that all afflictions are the Tathāgata seed.
Just as one cannot obtain priceless pearls without descending into the great ocean,
similarly, without entering the great ocean of afflictions,
one cannot obtain the treasure of omniscience.
Then Mahākāśyapa exclaimed,
"Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!
Well spoken indeed, just as you said.
The category of defilements constitutes the Tathāgata seed.
We now can no longer generate the mind of Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi.
Even those committing the five heinous crimes
can still generate the intention and produce the Buddha Dharma,
but we can never generate it.
Like a person with decayed roots who can no longer enjoy the five desires,
similarly, we Śrāvakas who have severed all bonds
can no longer benefit in the Buddha Dharma and have forever lost the aspiration.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī,
ordinary people have the potential to turn around in the Buddha Dharma,
while Śrāvakas do not.
Why is this?
Ordinary people hearing the Buddha Dharma can generate the supreme mind and not sever the Three Jewels.
Even if Śrāvakas hear throughout their lives about the Buddha's powers and fearlessness,
they can never generate the supreme intention."
Then in the assembly, there was a Bodhisattva named Universal Manifestation of Forms
who asked Vimalakīrti,
"Householder,
who are your parents, wife, children, relatives, retinue, officials, citizens, and acquaintances?
Where are your servants, attendants, elephants, horses, carriages, and vehicles?"
Then Vimalakīrti replied in verse:
Wisdom is the Bodhisattva's mother,
Expedient means are the father;
All guides of beings
Are born from these.
Dharma joy is the wife,
Compassionate mind the daughter,
Wholesome mind and honesty the son,
Ultimate emptiness and tranquility the home.
The disciples are the defilements,
Transformed at will;
The path factors are good friends,
Through them perfect enlightenment is attained.
The perfections are companions,
The four attractives are courtesans,
Chanting and singing Dharma words,
Using these as music.
The garden of retention,
The grove of undefiled Dharma,
The pure wonderful flowers of awakening,
The fruit of liberation and wisdom.
The bath pond of eight liberations,
Filled with serene water of concentration,
Spread with flowers of seven purities,
Bathing the undefiled person.
Elephant and horse of five penetrations galloping,
The Great Vehicle as the carriage,
Tamed and guided with single-mindedness,
Traveling the eightfold right path.
Marks complete to adorn the appearance,
All excellences decorating the form,
Robe of supreme shame and conscience,
Garland of profound mind.
Rich with seven treasures,
Teaching to nourish growth,
Practicing as spoken,
Dedication for great benefit.
The four meditations as seat and bed,
Born from pure livelihood,
Much learning increasing wisdom,
Serving as the sound of self-awakening.
The food of ambrosial Dharma,
The drink of liberation flavor,
Bathing with purified mind,
The perfume of moral discipline.
Destroying the thief of afflictions,
Courageous and invincible,
Subduing the four kinds of Māras,
Victorious banner erected at the path site.
Though knowing no arising or cessation,
Manifesting birth for their sake;
Fully revealing all lands,
Like the sun, seen everywhere.
Making offerings in the ten directions,
To countless billions of Tathāgatas,
Regarding Buddhas and oneself,
Without discriminative thoughts.
Though knowing all Buddha lands
And beings are empty,
Constantly cultivating pure lands,
Teaching and transforming all beings.
All kinds of beings,
Their forms, sounds, and dignified manners,
The fearless power Bodhisattva
Can simultaneously fully manifest.
Awake to Māra's activities,
Yet showing conformity to their ways;
With skillful expedient wisdom,
All can manifest at will.
Sometimes showing old age, sickness, death,
To mature all beings;
Fully knowing they are like illusions,
Penetrating without obstruction.
Sometimes manifesting conflagration at kalpa's end,
Heaven and earth all ablaze,
Beings holding notions of permanence,
Illumined to know impermanence.
Countless billions of beings
Together come inviting the Bodhisattva,
Simultaneously arriving at his abode,
Transformed to turn toward the Buddha Way.
Scriptures, spells, and arts,
Various crafts and skills,
Fully manifesting these activities,
Benefiting all beings.
All paths and methods in the world,
Fully ordaining within them,
Thereby resolving people's doubts,
Without falling into wrong views.
Sometimes becoming sun, moon, heaven,
Brahmā King, world ruler,
Sometimes becoming earth, water,
Or again becoming wind, fire.
When kalpas have epidemics,
Appearing as various medicinal herbs;
If there are those who take them,
Illnesses are cured, poisons dispelled.
When kalpas have famines,
Appearing as food and drink,
First saving them from hunger and thirst,
Then speaking Dharma to people.
When kalpas have warfare,
Generating compassion for it,
Transforming those beings,
Establishing them in non-contention.
If there are great battle arrays,
Establishing them with equal strength;
The Bodhisattva manifests majestic power,
Subduing and pacifying them.
In all lands,
Wherever there are hells,
Immediately going to those places,
Rescuing and relieving their sufferings.
In all lands,
Where animals eat each other,
Appearing born among them,
Bringing benefit to them.
He shows acceptance of the five desires,
Yet also practices meditation,
Causing the demon's mind to be confused and disturbed,
Unable to find an opportunity.
A lotus blooming in the midst of fire—
This can be called rare.
Practicing meditation amidst desires—
Is similarly rare.
Sometimes he appears as a courtesan,
Attracting those fond of beauty,
First engaging them with desire's hook,
Then leading them into the Buddha's path.
Sometimes as the lord of a city,
Or as a guide for merchants,
As a state preceptor or high minister,
To benefit and aid all beings.
For those who are impoverished,
He manifests as an inexhaustible treasury,
Thereby encouraging and guiding them,
To awaken the mind of enlightenment.
For those with arrogant minds,
He appears as a mighty warrior,
Subduing their pride,
Establishing them in the supreme path.
For those filled with fear,
He stands before them giving comfort,
First bestowing fearlessness,
Then inspiring the enlightened mind.
Sometimes he appears free from lust,
As a sage with five supernatural powers,
Guiding all living beings,
To abide in precepts, patience, and compassion.
Seeing those needing service,
He appears as a servant or attendant,
First pleasing them,
Then inspiring the enlightened mind.
According to what they require,
He enables their entry into the Buddha's path.
Through skillful means,
He fulfills all their needs.
Thus, the ways are limitless,
His practices without boundary,
His wisdom without measure,
Liberating countless beings.
Even if all Buddhas,
For countless eons,
Praised his virtues,
They could never exhaust them.
Who, hearing such Dharma,
Would not awaken the enlightened mind?
Except those base individuals,
Stupid and without wisdom.
At that time, Vimalakīrti
Addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas:
"Virtuous ones,
how does a bodhisattva enter the gate of non-duality?
Each may speak according to your understanding."
In the assembly was a bodhisattva named Dharma Sovereign,
who said:
"Virtuous ones,
birth and extinction are dual.
Dharma originally does not arise and now does not cease.
Attaining this patience of non-arising
is entering the gate of non-duality."
Virtue Guard Bodhisattva said:
"Self and mine are dual.
Because there is self, there is mine.
If there is no self, there is no mine.
This is entering the gate of non-duality."
Unblinking Bodhisattva said:
"Acceptance and non-acceptance are dual.
If dharma is not accepted, it cannot be grasped.
Because it cannot be grasped, there is no taking, no abandoning, no action, no practice.
This is entering the gate of non-duality."
Virtue Summit Bodhisattva said:
"Defilement and purity are dual.
Seeing the true nature of defilement, there is no purity, conforming to the nature of cessation.
This is entering the gate of non-duality."
Good Abode Bodhisattva said:
"Movement and thought are dual.
Without movement there is no thought.
Without thought there is no discrimination.
One who penetrates this
enters the gate of non-duality."
Good Eye Bodhisattva said:
"One mark and marklessness are dual.
Knowing one mark is marklessness,
not grasping marklessness, entering equality
is entering the gate of non-duality."
Wonderful Arm Bodhisattva said:
"Bodhisattva mind and śrāvaka mind are dual.
Observing mind's marks as empty like illusions,
no bodhisattva mind, no śrāvaka mind
is entering the gate of non-duality."
Fúshā Bodhisattva said:
"Good and not good are dual.
Not producing good or not good,
entering the realm of marklessness and penetrating it
is entering the gate of non-duality."
Lion Bodhisattva said:
"Sin and blessing are dual.
Penetrating sin's nature, it is no different from blessing.
With vajra wisdom understanding this mark - no bondage, no liberation
is entering the gate of non-duality."
Lion Mind Bodhisattva said:
"With outflows and without outflows are dual.
Attaining equality of all dharmas, no thought of outflow or no-outflow arises,
not attached to marks nor abiding in marklessness
is entering the gate of non-duality."
Pure Understanding Bodhisattva said:
"Conditioned and unconditioned are dual.
Transcending all calculations, mind becomes like space.
With pure wisdom unobstructed
is entering the gate of non-duality."
Nārāyaṇa Bodhisattva said:
"Worldly and world-transcending are dual.
Worldly nature empty is world-transcending.
In this, not entering, not emerging, not overflowing, not scattering
is entering the gate of non-duality."
Good Mind Bodhisattva said:
"Saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are dual.
Seeing saṃsāra's nature, there is no saṃsāra,
no bondage, no liberation, no birth, no cessation.
Understanding thus
is entering the gate of non-duality."
Direct Seeing Bodhisattva said:
"Exhaustion and non-exhaustion are dual.
Dharma ultimately exhausted or not exhausted are both inexhaustible marks.
Inexhaustible marks are emptiness.
Emptiness has no exhaustion or non-exhaustion marks.
Entering thus
is entering the gate of non-duality."
Universal Guard Bodhisattva said:
"Self and non-self are dual.
Self cannot be attained, how much less non-self?
Seeing self's true nature, duality no longer arises.
This is entering the gate of non-duality."
Lightning God Bodhisattva said:
"Enlightenment and ignorance are dual.
Ignorance's true nature is enlightenment.
Enlightenment too cannot be grasped, transcending all calculations.
In this equality without duality
is entering the gate of non-duality."
Joyful Seeing Bodhisattva said:
"Form and form's emptiness are dual.
Form is emptiness - not that form ceases to be empty; form's nature is naturally empty.
Similarly, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness and consciousness' emptiness are dual.
Consciousness is emptiness - not that consciousness ceases to be empty; consciousness' nature is naturally empty.
Penetrating this
is entering the gate of non-duality."
Bright Mark Bodhisattva said:
"The four elements different from space element is dual.
The four elements' nature is space element's nature.
As past and future boundaries are empty, so the present boundary is empty.
Knowing all elements' nature thus
is entering the gate of non-duality."
Wonderful Meaning Bodhisattva said:
"Eye and form are dual.
Knowing eye's nature, towards forms no greed, anger, or delusion arises.
This is called tranquil extinction.
Similarly, ear-sound, nose-smell, tongue-taste, body-touch, mind-dharma are dual.
Knowing mind's nature, towards dharmas no greed, anger, or delusion arises.
This is called tranquil extinction.
Abiding peacefully herein
is entering the gate of non-duality."
Inexhaustible Meaning Bodhisattva said:
"Giving and dedicating to omniscience are dual.
Giving's nature is dedicating to omniscience's nature.
Similarly, morality, patience, diligence, meditation, wisdom
dedicating to omniscience are dual.
Wisdom's nature is dedicating to omniscience's nature.
Entering single mark herein
is entering the gate of non-duality."
Profound Wisdom Bodhisattva said:
"Emptiness, marklessness, and wishlessness are dual.
Emptiness is marklessness, marklessness is wishlessness.
If empty, markless, wishless, then no mind, consciousness, or mental faculty.
One liberation gate is the three liberation gates
is entering the gate of non-duality."
Tranquil Root Bodhisattva said:
"Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha are dual.
Buddha is Dharma, Dharma is Saṅgha.
These three jewels are unconditioned marks, equal to space.
All dharmas are likewise.
Following this practice
is entering the gate of non-duality."
Unobstructed Mind Bodhisattva said:
"Body and body's cessation are dual.
Body is body's cessation.
Why?
Seeing body's true reality, one doesn't perceive body or body's cessation.
Body and body's cessation are neither dual nor different.
Herein unstartled, unafraid
is entering the gate of non-duality."
Bodhisattva Shàngshàn said:
Goodness of body, speech, and mind are dualistic.
These three activities are all without marks of action.
Body without marks of action is speech without marks of action.
Speech without marks of action is mind without marks of action.
These three activities without marks of action mean all phenomena are without marks of action.
One who can follow this wisdom of non-action
thereby enters the Dharma gate of non-duality.
Bodhisattva Fútián said:
Meritorious deeds, evil deeds, and immovable deeds are dualistic.
The true nature of these three deeds is emptiness.
Emptiness means no meritorious deeds, no evil deeds, no immovable deeds.
One who does not generate these three deeds
thereby enters the Dharma gate of non-duality.
Bodhisattva Huáyán said:
Arising from self is dualistic.
One who perceives the true reality of self does not generate dualistic dharmas.
If one does not abide in dualistic dharmas, there is no consciousness.
One without consciousness
thereby enters the Dharma gate of non-duality.
Bodhisattva Dézàng said:
Having the mark of attainment is dualistic.
Without attainment, there is no grasping or rejecting.
One without grasping or rejecting
thereby enters the Dharma gate of non-duality.
Bodhisattua Yuèshàng said:
Darkness and light are dualistic.
Without darkness or light, there is no duality.
Why is this?
Just as in the cessation of perception and feeling samādhi there is no darkness or light, so too are all dharmas.
One who enters this with equality
thereby enters the Dharma gate of non-duality.
Bodhisattva Bǎoyìnshǒu said:
Delighting in nirvāṇa and not delighting in the world is dualistic.
If one neither delights in nirvāṇa nor despises the world, there is no duality.
Why is this?
If there is bondage, there is liberation.
If fundamentally there is no bondage, who seeks liberation?
Without bondage or liberation, there is no delight or aversion.
This is entering the Dharma gate of non-duality.
Bodhisattva Zhūdǐngwáng said:
The right path and the wrong path are dualistic.
One abiding in the right path does not discriminate between wrong and right.
Transcending these two
thereby enters the Dharma gate of non-duality.
Bodhisattva Lèshí said:
Real and unreal are dualistic.
One with true sight does not even see the real, let alone the unreal.
Why is this?
It is not seen by the physical eye but by the wisdom eye.
Yet this wisdom eye neither sees nor does not see.
This is entering the Dharma gate of non-duality.
After each of these bodhisattvas had spoken,
they asked Mañjuśrī:
What is the bodhisattva's entry into the Dharma gate of non-duality?
Mañjuśrī said:
In my opinion,
regarding all dharmas, there is no speech, no explanation,
no indication, no recognition, transcending all questions and answers—this is entering the Dharma gate of non-duality. Then Mañjuśrī
asked Vimalakīrti:
We have each spoken;
you, benevolent one, should speak.
What is the bodhisattva's entry into the Dharma gate of non-duality?
At that time, Vimalakīrti remained silent, saying nothing.
Mañjuśrī exclaimed:
Excellent, excellent!
Even to have no written words or speech
is the true entry into the Dharma gate of non-duality.
When this chapter on entering the Dharma gate of non-duality was spoken,
five thousand bodhisattvas in the assembly
all entered the Dharma gate of non-duality and attained the patience of non-arising.
Then Śāriputra thought to himself:
The time is approaching;
where will these bodhisattvas eat?
Vimalakīrti,
knowing his thought, said:
The Buddha spoke of the eight liberations;
you, benevolent one, have practiced them.
How could you listen to the Dharma while mixed with desires for food?
If you wish to eat, wait a moment,
and I will give you food such as you have never had.
Then Vimalakīrti entered samādhi,
and through his spiritual power showed the great assembly
a realm beyond forty-two Ganges rivers' sands of buddha-lands
where there is a land called Fragrant Accumulation,
with a buddha named Fragrance Accumulated,
presently dwelling there.
The fragrance of that land surpasses all fragrances of humans and devas in the ten-direction buddha-worlds, being the foremost.
That land has no names of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas,
only pure multitudes of great bodhisattvas,
to whom the buddha preaches the Dharma.
Everything in that realm is made of fragrance: pavilions,
walking paths, fragrant grounds, gardens—all are fragrant.
The fragrance of their food pervades countless worlds in the ten directions.
At that time, that buddha was sitting and eating with the bodhisattvas.
There were devas all named Fragrant Adornment,
who had all aroused the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi,
making offerings to that buddha and the bodhisattvas.
Everyone in the great assembly saw this with their own eyes.
Then Vimalakīrti asked the assembled bodhisattvas:
Benevolent ones,
who can bring back food from that buddha?
Due to Mañjuśrī's majestic spiritual power, all remained silent.
Vimalakīrti said:
Are you not ashamed before this great assembly?
Mañjuśrī said:
As the Buddha said, do not despise the unlearned.
Then Vimalakīrti,
without rising from his seat, manifested a transformed bodhisattva before the assembly,
whose features, radiance, majesty, and virtue surpassed all in the assembly,
and told him:
Go to the realm above,
beyond forty-two Ganges rivers' sands of buddha-lands,
where there is a land called Fragrant Accumulation,
with a buddha named Fragrance Accumulated,
sitting and eating with the bodhisattvas.
Go there and say on my behalf:
Vimalakīrti bows at the World-Honored One's feet,
offering boundless reverence, inquiring after your well-being, any slight illness or trouble, and whether your strength is at ease.
I wish to receive the leftovers of the World-Honored One's meal
to perform buddha-work in the Sahā world,
enabling those attached to inferior teachings to expand into the great path,
and also making the Tathāgata's name universally known.
Then the transformed bodhisattva rose upward before the assembly.
All saw him go to the Fragrant Accumulation world and bow at that buddha's feet,
and heard him say:
Vimalakīrti bows at the World-Honored One's feet,
offering boundless reverence, inquiring after your well-being, any slight illness or trouble, and whether your strength is at ease.
I wish to receive the leftovers of the World-Honored One's meal
to perform buddha-work in the Sahā world,
enabling those attached to inferior teachings to expand into the great path,
and also making the Tathāgata's name universally known.
Those great beings, seeing the transformed bodhisattva, exclaimed in wonder,
"From where has this superior one come?
Where is the Sahā world?
What is meant by 'those attached to inferior teachings'?"
They asked the buddha.
The buddha told them:
Below, beyond forty-two Ganges rivers' sands of buddha-lands,
there is a world named Sahā,
with a buddha named Śākyamuni,
presently in the five turbid evil world,
expounding the Dharma for beings attached to inferior teachings.
There is a bodhisattva named Vimalakīrti,
dwelling in inconceivable liberation,
preaching the Dharma for bodhisattvas,
who sent this transformation to extol my name and praise this land,
to increase those bodhisattvas' merit.
Those bodhisattvas said:
What kind of person is he to manifest such a transformation?
With such virtue, power, fearlessness, and spiritual feats?
The buddha said:
Great indeed.
He sends transformations to all ten directions to perform buddha-work and benefit beings.
Then the Fragrance Accumulated Tathāgata
filled a fragrant bowl with fragrant food and gave it to the transformed bodhisattva.
At that time, nine million bodhisattvas there spoke in unison:
We wish to go to the Sahā world to make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha
and see Vimalakīrti and the other bodhisattvas.
The buddha said: You may go.
Restrain your body's fragrance,
lest those beings develop confused attachment.
Also, relinquish your original forms,
so that those in that land seeking bodhisattvahood do not feel ashamed.
And do not harbor contempt or obstructive thoughts toward them.
Why?
The lands of the ten directions are all like empty space.
Also, buddhas, to teach those attached to inferior teachings,
do not fully reveal their pure lands.
Then the transformed bodhisattva, having received the bowl of food,
together with those nine million bodhisattvas,
suddenly vanished from that world
and in a moment arrived at Vimalakīrti's dwelling.
Then Vimalakīrti
manifested nine million lion seats, as majestic and fine as before,
and all the bodhisattvas sat on them.
The transformed bodhisattva gave the full bowl of fragrant food to Vimalakīrti.
The food's fragrance pervaded the city of Vaiśālī and the three-thousand-great-thousand world.
Then the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī,
smelling this fragrance, felt physical and mental bliss and exclaimed in wonder.
Then the elder lord Yuègài,
with eighty-four thousand people, entered Vimalakīrti's dwelling.
Seeing the many bodhisattvas in his room and the lofty, broad, majestic lion seats, they
greatly rejoiced, bowed to the bodhisattvas and great disciples,
and stood to one side.
Various earth spirits, space spirits, and devas of the desire and form realms,
smelling this fragrance, also came into Vimalakīrti's dwelling.
Then Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra and the other great śrāvakas:
You may eat this Tathāgata's nectar-flavored food, perfumed by great compassion; do not eat it with limited minds, lest it not digest.
Some śrāvakas thought:
This food is little, yet everyone in this great assembly should eat.
The transformed bodhisattva said:
Do not measure the Tathāgata's boundless merit and wisdom with the śrāvakas' small virtue and wisdom.
The four seas may dry up, but this food is inexhaustible.
If all people ate portions as large as Mount Sumeru for a kalpa, it would still not be exhausted.
Why?
The leftovers from one fully endowed with inexhaustible precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and liberation knowledge
can never be exhausted.
Thus, the bowl of rice satisfied the entire assembly, yet it was not exhausted.
All the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, gods, and humans who ate this rice
experienced physical comfort and joy,
just like the bodhisattvas in the Land of Blissful Adornment.
Moreover, from all their pores emanated wondrous fragrances,
similar to the scents of the trees in the Land of Many Fragrances.
At that time, Vimalakīrti asked the bodhisattvas from the Fragrant Land:
"How does the Tathāgata of Fragrance Accumulation expound the Dharma?"
Those bodhisattvas replied:
"Our Tathāgata does not use words or texts.
He only uses various fragrances to enable gods and humans to observe the precepts.
Each bodhisattva sits under a fragrant tree, and upon smelling this exquisite fragrance,
immediately attains the samādhi of the Treasury of All Virtues.
Those who attain this samādhi
possess all the merits of a bodhisattva in full.
Then those bodhisattvas asked Vimalakīrti:
"How does the World-Honored One Śākyamuni expound the Dharma in this world?"
Vimalakīrti said:
"Because the beings in this land are stubborn and difficult to tame,
the Buddha uses stern language to subdue them.
He speaks of hells, animals, hungry ghosts,
and various unfortunate realms;
of places where foolish beings are born;
of physical misdeeds and their retributions;
of verbal misdeeds and their retributions;
of mental misdeeds and their retributions;
of killing and its retribution;
of stealing and its retribution;
of sexual misconduct and its retribution;
of false speech and its retribution;
of slander and its retribution;
of harsh speech and its retribution;
of frivolous speech and its retribution;
of covetousness and its retribution;
of anger and its retribution;
of wrong views and their retribution;
of stinginess and its retribution;
of breaking precepts and its retribution;
of hatred and its retribution;
of laziness and its retribution;
of distracted mind and its retribution;
of ignorance and its retribution;
of establishing precepts, keeping precepts, and violating precepts;
of what should be done and what should not be done;
of what is obstructive and what is not obstructive;
of what incurs offenses and what avoids offenses;
of purity and defilement;
of what is with outflows and what is without outflows;
of wrong paths and right paths;
of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena;
of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Because the minds of difficult-to-tame people are like monkeys,
various methods must be used to control and tame their minds.
Just as wild elephants and horses must be disciplined with severe punishment, even to the bone, before they can be tamed,
so too with stubborn, difficult-to-tame beings—
only through all kinds of harsh words can they be guided to observe the precepts."
Hearing this, those bodhisattvas
all exclaimed, "How unprecedented!
The World-Honored One Śākyamuni Buddha,
concealing his immeasurable sovereign powers,
uses methods suited to the poor to liberate beings.
These bodhisattvas too can toil humbly,
generating great compassion to be born in this buddha-land."
Vimalakīrti said:
"The bodhisattvas in this land have steadfast great compassion for all beings.
It is indeed as you say.
However, in one lifetime of benefiting beings here,
they accomplish more than in hundreds of thousands of kalpas in your land.
Why is this?
Because this Sahā world has ten wholesome dharmas
that other pure lands do not possess.
What are these ten?
Using giving to gather in the poor;
using pure precepts to gather in those who break precepts;
using patience to gather in the hateful;
using diligence to gather in the lazy;
using meditation to gather in the distracted;
using wisdom to gather in the ignorant;
teaching methods to eliminate difficulties and save those in the eight adversities;
using the Great Vehicle to save those attached to the Lesser Vehicle;
using good roots to aid the virtueless;
and constantly using the four means of embrace to mature beings.
These are the ten."
Those bodhisattvas asked:
"How many dharmas must a bodhisattva accomplish
to practice in this world without blemish and be reborn in a pure land?"
Vimalakīrti said:
"A bodhisattva who accomplishes eight dharmas
can practice in this world without blemish and be reborn in a pure land.
What are these eight?
Benefiting beings without expecting reward;
enduring all sufferings on behalf of beings;
dedicating all merits to others;
regarding all beings equally with humility and without obstruction;
viewing other bodhisattvas as buddhas;
hearing previously unlearned sūtras without doubt;
not conflicting with śrāvakas;
not envying others' offerings nor exalting one's own gain,
while therein taming one's mind;
constantly reflecting on one's own faults and not disputing others' shortcomings;
always single-mindedly seeking all merits.
These are the eight dharmas."
When Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī
expounded this Dharma in the great assembly,
hundreds of thousands of gods and humans aroused the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi,
and ten thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.
At that time, while the Buddha was expounding the Dharma in the Āmra Garden,
the ground suddenly became vast and magnificently adorned,
and the entire assembly turned golden.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"World-Honored One,
what is the cause for this auspicious sign?
This place has suddenly become vast and magnificently adorned,
and the entire assembly has turned golden."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"It is because Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī,
reverently surrounded by the great assembly,
are intending to come here, so this auspicious sign appears first."
Thereupon Vimalakīrti said to Mañjuśrī:
"Let us go together to see the Buddha and pay respects with the bodhisattvas."
Mañjuśrī said:
"Excellent! Let us go.
Now is the right time."
Vimalakīrti then used his supernatural power
to hold the great assembly and their lion thrones on his right palm,
and went to where the Buddha was. Upon arrival, he set them down,
bowed at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right,
joined his palms single-mindedly, and stood to one side.
The bodhisattvas all descended from their seats, bowed at the Buddha's feet,
also circumambulated seven times, and stood to one side.
The great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and others
also descended from their seats, bowed at the Buddha's feet, and stood to one side.
Then the World-Honored One, having duly greeted the bodhisattvas, asked them all to be seated again.
They all accepted the instruction, and when the assembly was seated,
the Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Do you see the sovereign supernatural powers of the great bodhisattva?"
"Indeed, I have seen.
What do you think of it?"
"World-Honored One,
I consider his deeds inconceivable—
beyond conceptual thought and measurement."
Then Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"World-Honored One,
the fragrance I smell now is unlike any I have known before.
What is this fragrance?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"It is the fragrance from the pores of those bodhisattvas."
Then Śāriputra said to Ānanda:
"Our pores also emit this fragrance."
Ānanda asked:
"Where does this come from?"
He replied:
"It is from the elder Vimalakīrti,
who brought leftover rice from the Buddha in the Land of Many Fragrances; those who ate it in his house
have all their pores fragrant like this."
Ānanda asked Vimalakīrti:
"How long will this fragrance last?"
Vimalakīrti said:
"Until the rice is digested."
Ānanda asked:
"How long until this rice is digested?"
He replied:
"The power of this rice lasts seven days, and then it is digested.
Moreover, Ānanda,
if śrāvakas who have not entered the right stage eat this rice,
they will enter the right stage before it is digested.
If those already in the right stage eat it,
they will attain liberation of mind before it is digested.
If those who have not aroused the mind of the Great Vehicle eat it,
they will arouse that mind before it is digested.
If those who have aroused that mind eat it,
they will attain the patience of non-arising before it is digested.
If those who have attained the patience of non-arising eat it,
they will reach the stage of one lifetime before buddhahood before it is digested.
Just as there is a medicine called Supreme Flavor that, when taken, eliminates all poisons in the body before being digested,
so this rice eliminates all afflictive poisons before being digested."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"How unprecedented!
World-Honored One,
such fragrant rice can perform buddha-work."
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is.
Ānanda,
some buddha-lands use the Buddha's light to perform buddha-work;
some use bodhisattvas;
some use people transformed by the Buddha;
some use the bodhi tree;
some use the Buddha's robes and bedding;
some use food and drink;
some use gardens, parks, towers, and pavilions;
some use the thirty-two marks and eighty excellent characteristics;
some use the Buddha's body;
some use empty space;
beings accordingly enter the precepts through these conditions.
Some use similes like dreams, illusions, shadows, echoes, images in mirrors, the moon in water, mirages, and so forth to perform buddha-work;
some use sounds, words, and texts;
some, in pure buddha-lands, use silence—no words, no speech, no showing, no recognition, no action, no doing—to perform buddha-work.
Thus, Ānanda,
all the Buddha's dignified manners and movements,
all his actions, are none other than buddha-work."
Ānán.
There are these four māras and eighty-four thousand gates of afflictions.
And all sentient beings are wearied by them.
The Buddhas use this very dharma to perform Buddha's work.
This is called entering the dharma gate of all Buddhas.
When bodhisattvas enter this gate,
if they see all pure and beautiful Buddha lands,
they do not rejoice, do not crave, and do not become haughty.
If they see all impure Buddha lands,
they do not grieve, are not obstructed, and do not sink.
They only give rise to a pure mind toward all Buddhas,
with joy, reverence, and unprecedented respect.
The merits and virtues of all Tathāgatas are equal.
For the sake of transforming sentient beings,
they manifest different Buddha lands.
Ānán,
you see that among the Buddha lands,
the earth may vary, but the sky does not vary.
Similarly, you see that the physical forms of the Buddhas may vary, but their unobstructed wisdom does not vary.
Ānán,
the physical forms, majestic marks, lineages,
precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation,
powers, fearlessnesses, and unique dharmas,
great compassion, great kindness, dignified conduct,
their lifespans, teaching of the dharma, and guidance,
the maturation of sentient beings, purification of Buddha lands,
and fulfillment of all Buddha dharmas—all are equal.
Therefore, they are called Samyaksaṃbuddha,
called Tathāgata,
called Buddha.
Ānán,
if I were to extensively explain the meaning of these three phrases,
you, even with a kalpa's lifespan, could not fully receive it.
Even if the entire trichiliocosm were filled with sentient beings
all like Ānán, foremost in learning and attaining mindfulness and dhāraṇī,
these people, even with a kalpa's lifespan, also could not receive it.
Thus, Ānán,
the Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi of all Buddhas is without limit,
their wisdom and eloquence are inconceivable.
Ānán said to the Buddha,
"From now on, I dare not consider myself as greatly learned."
The Buddha told Ānán,
"Do not give rise to a regressive mind.
Why?
I say that among the śrāvakas, you are the most learned,
but not among the bodhisattvas.
Enough, Ānán.
Those with wisdom should not measure the limits of bodhisattvas.
All oceans and abysses can still be measured,
but the meditative concentration, wisdom, dhāraṇī, eloquence, and all merits of bodhisattvas are immeasurable.
Ānán,
you should set aside the practices of bodhisattvas.
The power of spiritual penetrations displayed by Vimalakīrti in a single moment—
all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
even with exhaustive transformations over hundreds of thousands of kalpas, could not accomplish.
At that time, the bodhisattvas who had come from the Fragrant Land
joined their palms and said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One,
when we first saw this land, we gave rise to inferior thoughts.
Now we repent and reject such a mind.
Why?
The expedient means of the Buddhas are inconceivable.
For the sake of delivering sentient beings,
they manifest different Buddha lands according to what is appropriate.
So it is, World-Honored One.
We beg you to bestow a brief dharma, so that when we return to our land, we may remember the Tathāgata."
The Buddha told the bodhisattvas,
"There is the liberation dharma door of the exhaustible and inexhaustible. You should study it.
What is called exhaustible?
It is conditioned dharmas.
What is called inexhaustible?
It is unconditioned dharmas.
As for bodhisattvas,
they do not exhaust the conditioned nor abide in the unconditioned.
What is called not exhausting the conditioned?
It means not abandoning great compassion, not forsaking great kindness.
Deeply arousing the mind of all wisdom without negligence.
Teaching and transforming sentient beings without ever tiring.
Constantly mindful of practicing the four means of attraction.
Protecting and upholding the true dharma without sparing body or life.
Planting all roots of virtue without weariness.
Always abiding in resolve with skillful means and dedication.
Seeking the dharma untiringly, teaching it without stinginess.
Diligently making offerings to all Buddhas.
Entering birth and death without fear.
Regarding honor and disgrace, the mind is without sorrow or joy.
Not despising the unlearned, respecting learners as Buddhas.
Causing those fallen into afflictions to give rise to right mindfulness.
Not valuing the joy of solitude.
Not clinging to one's own joy, rejoicing in others' joy.
Regarding all meditative concentrations as like hell.
Regarding birth and death as like a pleasure garden.
Seeing those who come seeking as good teachers.
Renouncing all possessions while possessing the thought of all wisdom.
Seeing those who break precepts with a mind to rescue and protect.
Regarding the pāramitās as parents.
Regarding the dharmas of the path factors as kin.
Cultivating roots of virtue without limit.
Using the adornments of pure lands to perfect one's own Buddha land.
Practicing limitless giving, perfecting the marks of excellence.
Eradicating all evils, purifying body, speech, and mind.
Facing countless kalpas of birth and death with courageous resolve.
Hearing of the immeasurable virtues of Buddhas without tiring in aspiration.
Using the sword of wisdom to destroy the thieves of afflictions, emerging from the aggregates, sense bases, and elements.
Bearing the burden of sentient beings, eternally liberating them.
With great vigor, crushing the armies of māras.
Constantly seeking the wisdom of true reality without thought.
Regarding worldly dharmas, having few desires and knowing contentment.
Regarding supramundane dharmas, seeking them without satiation.
Without abandoning worldly dharmas, without breaking dignified conduct, yet able to follow customs.
Arousing the wisdom of spiritual powers to guide sentient beings.
Attaining mindfulness and dhāraṇī, never forgetting what is heard.
Skillfully discerning faculties, cutting off sentient beings' doubts.
With eloquence in joyful speech, expounding the dharma without obstruction.
Purifying the ten good paths, receiving heavenly and human blessings.
Cultivating the four immeasurables, opening the way to Brahmā heavens.
Encouraging the teaching of dharma, rejoicing in and praising goodness.
Attaining the Buddha's voice, goodness in body, speech, and mind.
Attaining the Buddha's dignified conduct, deeply cultivating good dharmas, with practices increasingly superior.
With the Mahāyāna teaching, forming the saṅgha of bodhisattvas.
The mind without negligence, not losing any goodness.
Practicing such dharmas—
this is called the bodhisattva not exhausting the conditioned.
What is called the bodhisattva not abiding in the unconditioned?
It means studying emptiness without taking emptiness as realization.
Studying signlessness and wishlessness,
without taking signlessness and wishlessness as realization.
Studying non-arising without taking non-arising as realization.
Contemplating impermanence without tiring of roots of goodness.
Contemplating the suffering of the world without loathing birth and death.
Contemplating selflessness while teaching others untiringly.
Contemplating cessation without eternally extinguishing.
Contemplating detachment while cultivating goodness with body and mind.
Contemplating no refuge while taking refuge in good dharmas.
Contemplating non-birth while bearing all with the dharma of birth.
Contemplating the non-outflow without severing all outflows.
Contemplating non-action while teaching sentient beings with the dharma of action.
Contemplating emptiness and nothingness without abandoning great compassion.
Contemplating the stage of true dharma without following the Hīnayāna.
Contemplating all dharmas as empty, false, without substance, without person, without master, without marks.
Without depleting merit, meditative concentration, and wisdom before original vows are fulfilled.
Cultivating such dharmas—
this is called the bodhisattva not abiding in the unconditioned.
Also, due to possessing merit, one does not abide in the unconditioned.
Due to possessing wisdom, one does not exhaust the conditioned.
Due to great compassion, one does not abide in the unconditioned.
Due to fulfilling original vows, one does not exhaust the conditioned.
Due to accumulating the medicine of dharma, one does not abide in the unconditioned.
Due to dispensing medicine accordingly, one does not exhaust the conditioned.
Due to knowing the illnesses of sentient beings, one does not abide in the unconditioned.
Due to extinguishing the illnesses of sentient beings, one does not exhaust the conditioned.
All noble bodhisattvas, by cultivating this dharma,
do not exhaust the conditioned nor abide in the unconditioned.
This is called the liberation dharma door of the exhaustible and inexhaustible.
You should study it."
At that time, those bodhisattvas, hearing this dharma, greatly rejoiced.
With various wonderful flowers of various colors and various scents,
they scattered them throughout the trichiliocosm,
making offerings to the Buddha, this sutra dharma, and all bodhisattvas. Then,
they bowed at the Buddha's feet and exclaimed with unprecedented praise,
"Śākyamuni Buddha
is able to skillfully practice expedient means here!"
Having spoken, they suddenly vanished and returned to their land.
Then the World-Honored One asked Vimalakīrti,
"You wish to see the Tathāgata.
How do you view the Tathāgata?"
Vimalakīrti said,
"As one views the true reality of one's own body,
so one views the Buddha.
I view the Tathāgata:
not coming from the past, not going to the future, not abiding in the present.
Not viewing form, not viewing form as such,
not viewing the nature of form.
Not viewing feeling, perception, formations, consciousness.
Not viewing consciousness as such,
not viewing the nature of consciousness.
Not arising from the four elements,
equal to space.
The six sense bases unaccumulated.
Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind—transcended, not dwelling in the three realms.
The three defilements already abandoned, in accord with the three gates of liberation.
Possessing the three clarities, equal to ignorance.
Not a single mark, not different marks.
Not self's mark, not other's mark.
Not without marks, not grasping marks.
Not this shore, not that shore, not in between.
Yet transforming sentient beings.
Contemplating cessation without eternal extinction.
Not this, not that.
Not by this, not by that.
Not knowable by wisdom,
not recognizable by consciousness.
Without darkness, without light, without name, without mark.
Without strength, without weakness, not pure, not impure.
Not in a location, not apart from location.
Not conditioned, not unconditioned.
Not demonstrated, not spoken."
Neither giving nor withholding.
Neither precept nor transgression.
Neither patience nor anger.
Neither diligence nor indolence.
Neither concentration nor distraction.
Neither wisdom nor ignorance.
Neither truthfulness nor deception.
Neither coming nor going.
Neither exiting nor entering.
All verbal paths are cut off.
Neither field of merit nor not field of merit.
Neither worthy of offerings nor unworthy of offerings.
Neither grasping nor abandoning.
Neither with form nor without form.
Identical with the true limit, equal to the nature of reality.
Inexpressible, immeasurable.
Surpassing all expressions and measurements.
Neither large nor small.
Neither seen, heard, perceived, nor known.
Free from all bonds.
Equal to all wisdoms, one with all beings.
Undifferentiated regarding all dharmas.
Nothing is lost.
Without defilement, without affliction.
Without action, without arising, without birth, without cessation.
Without fear, without sorrow, without joy, without aversion, without attachment.
Without past existence, without future existence, without present existence.
Cannot be expressed or differentiated by any words.
World-Honored One.
Such is the body of the Tathāgata.
To view it thus.
Such viewing is called right view.
Any other view is called wrong view.
Then Śāriputra asked Vimalakīrti,
"From which realm did you pass away and come to be born here?"
Vimalakīrti said,
"Is the Dharma you have attained subject to death and birth?"
Śāriputra said,
"It has no death or birth."
"If all dharmas have no characteristic of death and birth,
why do you ask, 'From which realm did you pass away and come to be born here?'
What do you think?
For example, when a magician creates an illusory man or woman,
do they undergo death and birth?"
Śāriputra said,
"They have no death or birth."
"Have you not heard the Buddha say all dharmas are like illusions?"
He replied, "Yes."
"If all dharmas are like illusions,
why do you ask, 'From which realm did you pass away and come to be born here?'
Śāriputra,
'Death' is the characteristic of decay in deceptive dharmas;
'Birth' is the characteristic of continuity in deceptive dharmas.
Though a bodhisattva dies, they do not exhaust their roots of virtue;
though born, they do not increase evils."
Then the Buddha told Śāriputra,
"There is a land named Wonderful Joy,
whose Buddha is called Immovable.
Vimalakīrti passed away from that land and was born here."
Śāriputra said,
"How extraordinary!
World-Honored One,
that this person could abandon a pure land
and come to take pleasure in this place full of anger and harm."
Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra,
"What do you think?
When sunlight appears, does it unite with darkness?"
He replied,
"No,
when sunlight appears, all darkness vanishes."
Vimalakīrti said,
"Why does the sun journey over Jambudvīpa?"
He replied, "To illuminate and dispel darkness."
Vimalakīrti said,
"So it is with a bodhisattva:
though born in an impure Buddha-land to teach beings, they do not unite with foolish darkness,
but only extinguish the darkness of beings' afflictions."
Then the assembly fervently longed
to see the Wonderful Joy world, Immovable Tathāgata, and his assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts of all present,
said to Vimalakīrti,
"Good man,
for this assembly,
manifest the Wonderful Joy land, Immovable Tathāgata, and his bodhisattvas and śrāvakas,
whom all wish to see."
Then Vimalakīrti thought,
"Without rising from my seat, I shall bring the Wonderful Joy land here—
its iron-ring mountains, rivers, valleys, streams,
great seas, springs, Mount Sumerus and other peaks,
sun, moon, and stars,
palaces of dragons, spirits, ghosts, and Brahmā gods,
along with its bodhisattvas and śrāvakas,
cities, towns, villages, men, women, great and small,
even Immovable Tathāgata, his bodhi tree, and exquisite lotuses,
all performing Buddha-works in the ten directions—
and the three jeweled stairways from Jambudvīpa to Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, by which gods descend
to pay homage to Immovable Tathāgata and hear the Dharma,
while humans of Jambudvīpa
also ascend
to Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to see those gods.
The Wonderful Joy world possesses such immeasurable merits, reaching up to Akaniṣṭha Heaven
and down to the water's edge.
With my right hand, I shall take it as a potter takes a wheel,
and bring it into this world like holding a flower garland to show all."
Having thought this, he entered samādhi and displayed supernatural power,
using his right hand to take the Wonderful Joy world and place it in this land.
Those with supernatural powers there—bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and other gods—
all cried out,
"Ah, World-Honored One!
Who is taking us away?
Save us!"
Immovable Buddha said,
"It is not my doing,
but the power of Vimalakīrti.
Those without supernatural powers
remained unaware of their movement.
Though entering this land, the Wonderful Joy world did not expand or shrink;
nor did this world become cramped, remaining as before."
Then Śākyamuni Buddha addressed the great assembly,
"Behold the Wonderful Joy world and Immovable Tathāgata—its splendid adornments,
pure practices of bodhisattvas, and stainless disciples."
All said,
"Yes, we see."
The Buddha said,
"If bodhisattvas wish to attain such a pure Buddha-land,
they should practice the path of Immovable Tathāgata."
When this Wonderful Joy land was manifested,
fourteen nayutas of beings in the Sahā world resolved on Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi,
all vowing rebirth in the Wonderful Joy Buddha-land.
Śākyamuni Buddha then predicted,
"They will be born there."
After the Wonderful Joy world had fulfilled its beneficial purpose here,
it returned to its original place, witnessed by all.
The Buddha asked Śāriputra,
"Have you seen the Wonderful Joy world and Immovable Buddha?"
"Yes, I have seen,
World-Honored One.
May all beings attain pure lands like Immovable Buddha's,
and gain supernatural powers like Vimalakīrti's.
World-Honored One,
we are greatly blessed
to see and serve this person.
Beings now or after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa
who hear this sūtra will also gain great blessing,
especially those who, upon hearing, believe, understand, uphold, recite, explain, and practice it accordingly.
Those who obtain this sūtra
have obtained the treasury of the Dharma jewel.
Those who recite, explain its meaning, and practice as taught
are protected and mindful by all Buddhas.
Those who make offerings to such persons
thereby make offerings to the Buddha.
Those who keep this sūtra
have the Tathāgata in their abode.
Those who rejoice upon hearing this sūtra
thereby grasp omniscience.
Those who believe, understand even a four-line verse, and teach others
are thereby predicted to attain Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi."
Then Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha before the assembly,
"World-Honored One,
